blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS 1

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered
irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We
begin with two very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2 and 1.3,
namely the Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Euclid's division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of
integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer $a$ can be divided by another positive
integer $b$ in such a way that it leaves a remainder $r$ that is smaller than $b$. Many of you
probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite
easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties
of integers. We touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF of
two positive integers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something
with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number
can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way — this important fact is the
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and
understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics.
We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we
use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as
$\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ . Second, we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal
expansion of a rational number, say $\frac{p}{q}(q \neq 0)$, is terminating and when it is non-
terminating repeating. We do so by looking at the prime factorisation of the denominator
$q$ of $\frac{p}{q}$ . You will see that the prime factorisation of $q$ will completely reveal the nature
of the decimal expansion of $\frac{p}{q}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So let us begin our exploration.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.2 Euclid's Division Lemma

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Consider the following folk puzzle*.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A trader was moving along a road selling eggs. An idler who didn't have
much work to do, started to get the trader into a wordy duel. This grew into a
fight, he pulled the basket with eggs and dashed it on the floor. The eggs broke.
The trader requested the Panchayat to ask the idler to pay for the broken eggs.
The Panchayat asked the trader how many eggs were broken. He gave the
following response:

blocks.label: Paragraph
Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, how many eggs were there? Let us try and solve the puzzle. Let the number
of eggs be $a$. Then working backwards, we see that $a$ is less than or equal to 150:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If counted in sevens, nothing will remain, which translates to $a = 7p + 0$, for
some natural number $p$. If counted in sixes, $a = 6q + 5$, for some natural number $q$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If counted in fives, four will remain. It translates to $a = 5w + 4$, for some natural
number $w$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If counted in fours, three will remain. It translates to $a = 4s + 3$, for some natural
number $s$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If counted in threes, two will remain. It translates to $a = 3t + 2$, for some natural
number $t$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If counted in pairs, one will remain. It translates to $a = 2u + 1$, for some natural
number $u$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
That is, in each case, we have $a$ and a positive integer $b$ (in our example,
$b$ takes values $7, 6, 5, 4, 3$ and $2$, respectively) which divides $a$ and leaves a remainder
$r$ (in our case, $r$ is $0, 5, 4, 3, 2$ and $1$, respectively), that is smaller than $b$. The

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * This is modified form of a puzzle given in ‘Numeracy Counts!’ by A. Rampal, and others.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
moment we write down such equations we are using Euclid's division lemma,
which is given in Theorem 1.1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Getting back to our puzzle, do you have any idea how you will solve it? Yes! You
must look for the multiples of 7 which satisfy all the conditions. By trial and error
(using the concept of LCM), you will find he had 119 eggs.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In order to get a feel for what Euclid's division lemma is, consider the following
pairs of integers:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Like we did in the example, we can write the following relations for each such
pair:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$17 = 6 \times 2 + 5 \ (6 \ goes \ into \ 17 \ twice \ and \ leaves \ a \ remainder \ 5)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$5 = 12 \times 0 + 5 \ (\text{This relation holds since } 12 \text{ is larger than } 5)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$20 = 4 \times 5 + 0 \ (\text{Here } 4 \text{ goes into } 20 \text{ five-times and leaves no remainder})$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
That is, for each pair of positive integers $a$ and $b$, we have found whole numbers
$q$ and $r$, satisfying the relation:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$a = bq + r, 0 \le r < b$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Note that $q$ or $r$ can also be zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Why don't you now try finding integers $a$ and $r$ for the following pairs of positive
integers $a$ and $b$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Did you notice that $q$ and $r$ are unique? These are the only integers satisfying the
conditions $a = bq + r$, where $0 \le r < b$. You may have also realised that this is nothing
but a restatement of the long division process you have been doing all these years, and
that the integers $q$ and $r$ are called the quotient and remainder, respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: A formal statement of this result is as follows :

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Theorem 1.1 (Euclid's Division Lemma) : Given positive integers $a$ and $b$,
there exist unique integers $q$ and $r$ satisfying $a = bq + r$, $0 \le r < b$.
This result was perhaps known for a long time, but was first recorded in Book VII
of Euclid's Elements. Euclid's division algorithm is based on this lemma.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
An algorithm is a series of well defined steps
which gives a procedure for solving a type of
problem.

The word algorithm comes from the name
of the 9th century Persian mathematician
al-Khwarizmi. In fact, even the word ‘algebra’
is derived from a book, he wrote, called Hisab
al-jabr w’al-muqabala.

A lemma is a proven statement used for
proving another statement.

Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi
(C.E. 780 – 850)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Euclid's division algorithm is a technique to compute the Highest Common Factor
(HCF) of two given positive integers. Recall that the HCF of two positive integers $a$
and $b$ is the largest positive integer $d$ that divides both $a$ and $b$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see how the algorithm works, through an example first. Suppose we need
to find the HCF of the integers 455 and 42. We start with the larger integer, that is,
455. Then we use Euclid's lemma to get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now consider the divisor 42 and the remainder 35, and apply the division lemma
to get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now consider the divisor 35 and the remainder 7, and apply the division lemma
to get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Notice that the remainder has become zero, and we cannot proceed any further.
We claim that the HCF of 455 and 42 is the divisor at this stage, i.e., 7. You can easily
verify this by listing all the factors of 455 and 42. Why does this method work? It
works because of the following result.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, let us state Euclid's division algorithm clearly.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To obtain the HCF of two positive integers, say $c$ and $d$, with $c > d$, follow
the steps below:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
Step 1 : Apply Euclid's division lemma, to $c$ and $d$. So, we find whole numbers, $q$ and
$r$ such that $c = dq + r$, $0 \le r < d$.
Step 2 : If $r=0$, $d$ is the HCF of $c$ and $d$. If $r \neq 0$, apply the division lemma to $d$ and $r$.
Step 3 : Continue the process till the remainder is zero. The divisor at this stage will
be the required HCF.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This algorithm works because HCF $(c, d) = \text{HCF} (d, r)$ where the symbol
$\text{HCF} (c, d)$ denotes the HCF of $c$ and $d$, etc.

get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 3 : We consider the new divisor 420 and the new remainder 272, and apply the
division lemma to get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We consider the new divisor 272 and the new remainder 148, and apply the division
lemma to get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We consider the new divisor 148 and the new remainder 124, and apply the division

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We consider the new divisor 124 and the new remainder 24, and apply the division

The remainder has now become zero, so our procedure stops. Since the divisor at this

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Euclid's division algorithm is not only useful for calculating the HCF of very
large numbers, but also because it is one of the earliest examples of an algorithm that
a computer had been programmed to carry out.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Euclid's division lemma and algorithm are so closely interlinked that people often
call former as the division algorithm also.
2. Although Euclid's Division Algorithm is stated for only positive integers, it can be
extended for all integers except zero, i.e., $b \neq 0$. However, we shall not discuss this
aspect here.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Euclid's division lemma/algorithm has several applications related to finding
properties of numbers. We give some examples of these applications below:

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 2} : Show that every positive even integer is of the form $2q$, and that every
positive odd integer is of the form $2q + 1$, where $q$ is some integer.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\underline{Solution} : Let $a$ be any positive integer and $b = 2$. Then, by Euclid's algorithm,
$a = 2q + r$, for some integer $q \ge 0$, and $r = 0$ or $r = 1$, because $0 \le r < 2$. So,
$a = 2q$ or $2q + 1$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $a$ is of the form $2q$, then $a$ is an even integer. Also, a positive integer can be
either even or odd. Therefore, any positive odd integer is of the form $2q + 1$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Show that any positive odd integer is of the form $4q + 1$ or $4q + 3$, where
$q$ is some integer.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let us start with taking $a$, where $a$ is a positive odd integer. We apply the
division algorithm with $a$ and $b=4$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since $0 \le r < 4$, the possible remainders are 0, 1, 2 and 3.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
That is, $a$ can be $4q$, or $4q + 1$, or $4q + 2$, or $4q + 3$, where $q$ is the quotient.
However, since $a$ is odd, $a$ cannot be $4q$ or $4q + 2$ (since they are both divisible by $2$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, any odd integer is of the form $4q + 1$ or $4q + 3$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : A sweetseller has 420 $kaju$ $barfis$ and 130 $badam$ $barfis$. She wants to
stack them in such a way that each stack has the same number, and they take up the
least area of the tray. What is the number of that can be placed in each stack for this
purpose?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : This can be done by trial and error. But to do it systematically, we find
HCF (420, 130). Then this number will give the maximum number of barfis in each
stack and the number of stacks will then be the least. The area of the tray that is used
up will be the least.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, let us use Euclid's algorithm to find their HCF. We have :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the HCF of 420 and 130 is 10.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the sweetseller can make stacks of 10 for both kinds of barfi.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.3 The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a
product of its prime factors. For instance, $2 = 2, 4 = 2 \times 2, 253 = 11 \times 23$, and so on.
Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any
natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Take any collection of prime numbers, say $2, 3, 7, 11$ and $23$. If we multiply
some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish,
we can produce a large collection of positive integers (In fact, infinitely many).
Let us list a few :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$7 \times 11 \times 23 = 1771$          $3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 5313$
$2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 10626$     $2^2 \times 3 \times 7^3 = 8232$
$2^2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 21252$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes.
What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite
number of integers, or infinitely many? Infact, there are infinitely many primes. So, if
we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite collection of
numbers, all the primes and all possible products of primes. The question is – can we
produce all the composite numbers this way? What do you think? Do you think that
there may be a composite number which is not the product of powers of primes?
Before we answer this, let us factorise positive integers, that is, do the opposite of
what we have done so far.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We are going to use the factor tree with which you are all familiar. Let us take
some large number, say, 32760, and factorise it as shown :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So we have factorised $32760$ as $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of
primes, i.e., $32760 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of powers of primes. Let us try
another number, say, $123456789$. This can be written as $3^2 \times 3803 \times 3607$. Of course,
you have to check that $3803$ and $3607$ are primes! (Try it out for several other natural
numbers yourself.) This leads us to a conjecture that every composite number can be
written as the product of powers of primes. In fact, this statement is true, and is called
the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic because of its basic crucial importance
to the study of integers. Let us now formally state this theorem.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Theorem 1.2 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) : Every composite number
can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is
unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
An equivalent version of Theorem 1.2 was probably first
recorded as Proposition 14 of Book IX in Euclid's
Elements, before it came to be known as the Fundamental
Theorem of Arithmetic. However, the first correct proof
was given by Carl Friedrich Gauss in his *Disquisitiones*
*Arithmeticae.*
Carl Friedrich Gauss is often referred to as the 'Prince of
Mathematicians' and is considered one of the three
greatest mathematicians of all time, along with Archimedes
and Newton. He has made fundamental contributions to
both mathematics and science.

Carl Friedrich Gauss
(1777 - 1855)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number
can be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given
any composite number it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a
‘unique’ way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any
composite number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes,
as long as we are not particular about the order in which the primes occur. So, for
example, we regard $2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7$ as the same as $3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 2$, or any other
possible order in which these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the
following form:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order
of its factors.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, given a composite number $x$, we factorise it as $x = p_1 p_2 ... p_n$, where
$p_1, p_2, ..., p_n$ are primes and written in ascending order, i.e., $p_1 \le p_2$
$\le ... \le p_n$. If we combine the same primes, we will get powers of primes. For example,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$32760 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number
is factorised, is unique.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has many applications, both within
mathematics and in other fields. Let us look at some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 5} : Consider the numbers $4^n$, where $n$ is a natural number. Check whether
there is any value of $n$ for which $4^n$ ends with the digit zero.

\underline{Solution} : If the number $4^n$, for any $n$, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be
divisible by 5. That is, the prime factorisation of $4^n$ would contain the prime 5. This is

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
not possible because $4^n = (2)^{2^n}$; so the only prime in the factorisation of $4^n$ is $2$. So, the
uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no
other primes in the factorisation of $4^n$. So, there is no natural number $n$ for which $4^n$
ends with the digit zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers
using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes, without realising it!
This method is also called the prime factorisation method. Let us recall this method
through an example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.
Solution : We have :      $6 = 2^1 \times 3^1$ and $20 = 2 \times 2 \times 5 = 2^2 \times 5^1$.
You can find HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$, as done in your
earlier classes.
Note that HCF(6, 20) = $2^1$ = Product of the smallest power of each common
prime factor in the numbers.
LCM (6, 20) = $2^2 \times 3^1 \times 5^1$ = Product of the greatest power of each prime factor,
involved in the numbers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the example above, you might have noticed that HCF$(6, 20) \times \text{LCM}(6, 20)$
$= 6 \times 20$. In fact, we can verify that for any two positive integers $a$ and $b$,
$\mathbf{HCF} (a, b) \times \mathbf{LCM} (a, b) = a \times b$. We can use this result to find the LCM of two
positive integers, if we have already found the HCF of the two positive integers.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : Find the HCF of 96 and 404 by the prime factorisation method. Hence,
find their LCM.

Solution : The prime factorisation of 96 and 404 gives :
$$96 = 2^5 \times 3, 404 = 2^2 \times 101$$
Therefore, the HCF of these two integers is $2^2 = 4$.

Also, $\text{LCM} (96, 404) = \frac{96 \times 404}{\text{HCF}(96, 404)} = \frac{96 \times 404}{4} = 9696$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 8 : Find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120, using the prime factorisation
method.
Solution : We have :
$$6 = 2 \times 3, 72 = 2^3 \times 3^2, 120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5$$
Here, $2^1$ and $3^1$ are the smallest powers of the common factors 2 and 3, respectively.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$2^1$, $3^2$ and $5^1$ are the greatest powers of the prime factors 2, 3 and 5 respectively
involved in the three numbers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Notice, $6 \times 72 \times 120 \neq HCF (6, 72, 120) \times LCM (6, 72, 120)$. So, the
product of three numbers is not equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.4 Revisiting Irrational Numbers

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you were introduced to irrational numbers and many of their properties.
You studied about their existence and how the rationals and the irrationals together
made up the real numbers. You even studied how to locate irrationals on the number
line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals. In this section, we will
prove that $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5}$ and, in general, $\sqrt{p}$ is irrational, where $p$ is a prime. One of
the theorems, we use in our proof, is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall, a number '$s$' is called \textit{irrational} if it cannot be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$,
where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \neq 0$. Some examples of irrational numbers, with

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which you are already familiar, are :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Before we prove that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, we need the following theorem, whose
proof is based on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Theorem 1.3 :** Let $p$ be a prime number. If $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$, where
$a$ is a positive integer.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: *Proof : Let the prime factorisation of $a$ be as follows :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $a = p_1 p_2 \dots p_n$, where $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$ are primes, not necessarily distinct.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a^2 = (p_1 p_2 \dots p_n)(p_1 p_2 \dots p_n) = p_1^2 p_2^2 \dots p_n^2.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, we are given that $p$ divides $a^2$. Therefore, from the Fundamental Theorem of
Arithmetic, it follows that $p$ is one of the prime factors of $a^2$. However, using the
uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, we realise that the only
prime factors of $a^2$ are $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$. So $p$ is one of $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, since $a = p_1 p_2 \dots p_n$, $p$ divides $a$. \hfill $\blacksquare$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We are now ready to give a proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The proof is based on a technique called 'proof by contradiction'. (This technique is
discussed in some detail in Appendix 1).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{Theorem 1.4 :} $\sqrt{2}$ \textit{is irrational.}
\textbf{Proof :} Let us assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.
So, we can find integers $r$ and $s$ $(\neq 0)$ such that $\sqrt{2} = \frac{r}{s}$.
Suppose $r$ and $s$ have a common factor other than 1. Then, we divide by the common
factor to get $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are coprime.
So, $b\sqrt{2} = a$.
Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get $2b^2 = a^2$. Therefore, 2 divides $a^2$.
Now, by Theorem 1.3, it follows that 2 divides $a$.
So, we can write $a = 2c$ for some integer $c$.

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * Not from the examination point of view.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting for $a$, we get $2b^2 = 4c^2$, that is, $b^2 = 2c^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This means that 2 divides $b^2$, and so 2 divides $b$ (again using Theorem 1.3 with $p=2$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a$ and $b$ have at least $2$ as a common factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $a$ and $b$ have no common factors other than 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 9 : Prove that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: That is, we can find integers $a$ and $b$ $(\neq 0)$ such that $\sqrt{3} = \frac{a}{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose $a$ and $b$ have a common factor other than $1$, then we can divide by the
common factor, and assume that $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, $b\sqrt{3} = a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Squaring on both sides, and rearranging, we get $3b^2 = a^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, $a^2$ is divisible by 3, and by Theorem 1.3, it follows that $a$ is also divisible
by 3.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can write $a = 3c$ for some integer $c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting for $a$, we get $3b^2 = 9c^2$, that is, $b^2 = 3c^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This means that $b^2$ is divisible by 3, and so $b$ is also divisible by 3 (using Theorem 1.3
with $p = 3$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a$ and $b$ have at least $3$ as a common factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.
So, we conclude that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In Class IX, we mentioned that :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ the sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational and
$\bullet$ the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and irrational number is
irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We prove some particular cases here.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 10 : Show that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: That is, we can find coprime $a$ and $b$ ($b \neq 0$) such that $5 - \sqrt{3} = \frac{a}{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $5 - \frac{a}{b} = \sqrt{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Rearranging this equation, we get $\sqrt{3} = 5 - \frac{a}{b} = \frac{5b - a}{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since $a$ and $b$ are integers, we get $5 - \frac{a}{b}$ is rational, and so $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is
rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 11} : Show that $3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
\underline{Solution} : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $3\sqrt{2}$ is rational.
That is, we can find coprime $a$ and $b$ $(b \neq 0)$ such that $3\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$.
Rearranging, we get $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{3b}$.
Since $3$, $a$ and $b$ are integers, $\frac{a}{3b}$ is rational, and so $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.
But this contradicts the fact that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
So, we conclude that $3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.5 Revisiting Rational Numbers and Their Decimal Expansions

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you studied that rational numbers have either a terminating decimal
expansion or a non-terminating repeating decimal expansion. In this section, we are
going to consider a rational number, say $\frac{p}{q}(q \neq 0)$, and explore exactly when the
decimal expansion of $\frac{p}{q}$ is terminating and when it is non-terminating repeating
(or recurring). We do so by considering several examples.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider the following rational numbers :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As one would expect, they can all be expressed as rational numbers whose
denominators are powers of 10. Let us try and cancel the common factors between
the numerator and denominator and see what we get :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Do you see any pattern? It appears that, we have converted a real number
whose decimal expansion terminates into a rational number of the form $\frac{p}{q}$, where $p$
and $q$ are coprime, and the prime factorisation of the denominator (that is, $q$) has only
powers of $2$, or powers of $5$, or both. We should expect the denominator to look like
this, since powers of $10$ can only have powers of $2$ and $5$ as factors.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Even though, we have worked only with a few examples, you can see that any
real number which has a decimal expansion that terminates can be expressed as a
rational number whose denominator is a power of 10. Also the only prime factors of 10
are 2 and 5. So, cancelling out the common factors between the numerator and the
denominator, we find that this real number is a rational number of the form $\frac{p}{q}$, where
the prime factorisation of $q$ is of the form $2^n 5^m$, and $n, m$ are some non-negative integers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us write our result formally:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Theorem 1.5 :** Let $x$ be a rational number whose decimal expansion terminates.
Then $x$ can be expressed in the form $\frac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are coprime, and the
prime factorisation of $q$ is of the form $2^{n}5^m$, where $n, m$ are non-negative integers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You are probably wondering what happens the other way round in Theorem 1.5.
That is, if we have a rational number of the form $\frac{p}{q}$, and the prime factorisation of $q$
is of the form $2^{x}5^x$, where $x, m$ are non negative integers, then does $\frac{p}{q}$ have a
terminating decimal expansion?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see if there is some obvious reason why this is true. You will surely agree
that any rational number of the form $\frac{a}{b}$, where $b$ is a power of 10, will have a terminating
decimal expansion. So it seems to make sense to convert a rational number of the
form $\frac{p}{q}$, where $q$ is of the form $2^{5}m$, to an equivalent rational number of the form $\frac{a}{b}$,
where $b$ is a power of 10. Let us go back to our examples above and work backwards.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, these examples show us how we can convert a rational number of the form
$\frac{p}{q}$, where $q$ is of the form $2^{n}5^m$, to an equivalent rational number of the form $\frac{a}{b}$,
where $b$ is a power of 10. Therefore, the decimal expansion of such a rational number
terminates. Let us write down our result formally.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\textbf{Theorem 1.6} : Let $x = \frac{p}{q}$ be a rational number, such that the prime factorisation
of $q$ is of the form $2^{n}5^n$, where $n, m$ are non-negative integers. Then $x$ has a
decimal expansion which terminates.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We are now ready to move on to the rational numbers
whose decimal expansions are non-terminating and recurring.
Once again, let us look at an example to see what is going on.
We refer to Example 5, Chapter 1, from your Class IX
textbook, namely, $\frac{1}{7}$ . Here, remainders are 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$
\begin{array}{r}
0.1428571 \\
7 \overline{) 10} \\
\underline{7} \\
\textcircled{2} 0 \\
\underline{28} \\
\textcircled{2} 0 \\
\underline{14} \\
\textcircled{6} 0 \\
\underline{56} \\
\textcircled{4} 0 \\
\underline{35} \\
\textcircled{5} 0 \\
\underline{49} \\
\textcircled{1} 0 \\
\underline{7} \\
\textcircled{3} 0
\end{array}
$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $2, 6, 4, 5, 1, \dots$ and divisor is $7$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Notice that the denominator here, i.e., 7 is clearly not of
the form $2^{75n}$. Therefore, from Theorems 1.5 and 1.6, we
know that $\frac{1}{7}$ will not have a terminating decimal expansion.
Hence, 0 will not show up as a remainder (Why?), and the
remainders will start repeating after a certain stage. So, we
will have a block of digits, namely, 142857, repeating in the
quotient of $\frac{1}{7}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What we have seen, in the case of $\frac{1}{7}$, is true for any rational number not covered
by Theorems 1.5 and 1.6. For such numbers we have :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\textbf{Theorem 1.7} : Let $x = \frac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ are coprimes, be a rational number, such
that the prime factorisation of $q$ is not of the form $2^n 5^n$, where $n, m$ are non-negative
integers. Then, $x$ has a decimal expansion which is non-terminating repeating
(recurring).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the discussion above, we can conclude that the decimal expansion of
every rational number is either terminating or non-terminating repeating.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.6 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Euclid's division lemma :
Given positive integers $a$ and $b$, there exist whole numbers $q$ and $r$ satisfying $a = bq + r$,
$0 \le r < b$.

2. Euclid's division algorithm : This is based on Euclid's division lemma. According to this,
the HCF of any two positive integers $a$ and $b$, with $a > b$, is obtained as follows:
Step 1 : Apply the division lemma to find $q$ and $r$ where $a = bq + r$, $0 \le r < b$.
Step 2 : If $r=0$, the HCF is $b$. If $r \ne 0$, apply Euclid's lemma to $b$ and $r$.
Step 3 : Continue the process till the remainder is zero. The divisor at this stage will be
HCF $(a, b)$. Also, $\text{HCF}(a, b) = \text{HCF}(b, r)$.

3. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic :
Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this
factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

4. If $p$ is a prime and $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$, where $a$ is a positive integer.

5. To prove that $\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}$ are irrationals.

6. Let $x$ be a rational number whose decimal expansion terminates. Then we can express $x$
in the form $\frac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are coprime, and the prime factorisation of $q$ is of the form
$2^{n}5^m$, where $n, m$ are non-negative integers.

7. Let $x = \frac{p}{q}$ be a rational number, such that the prime factorisation of $q$ is of the form $2^{n}5^m$,
where $n, m$ are non-negative integers. Then $x$ has a decimal expansion which terminates.

8. Let $x = \frac{p}{q}$ be a rational number, such that the prime factorisation of $q$ is not of the form
$2^n 5^m$, where $n, m$ are non-negative integers. Then $x$ has a decimal expansion which is
non-terminating repeating (recurring).

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
A NOTE TO THE READER

You have seen that :

$$HCF(p, q, r) \times LCM(p, q, r) \neq p \times q \times r, \text{ where } p, q, r \text{ are positive integers}$$
(see Example 8). However, the following results hold good for three numbers
$p, q$ and $r$ :

$$LCM(p, q, r) = \frac{p \cdot q \cdot r \cdot HCF(p, q, r)}{HCF(p, q) \cdot HCF(q, r) \cdot HCF(p, r)}$$

$$HCF(p, q, r) = \frac{p \cdot q \cdot r \cdot LCM(p, q, r)}{LCM(p, q) \cdot LCM(q, r) \cdot LCM(p, r)}$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you have studied polynomials in one variable and their degrees. Recall
that if $p(x)$ is a polynomial in $x$, the highest power of $x$ in $p(x)$ is called the **degree of**
**the polynomial** $p(x)$. For example, $4x + 2$ is a polynomial in the variable $x$ of
degree $1$, $2y^2 - 3y + 4$ is a polynomial in the variable $y$ of degree $2$, $5x^3 - 4x^2 + x - \sqrt{2}$
is a polynomial in the variable $x$ of degree $3$ and $7u^6 - \frac{3}{2}u^4 + 4u^2 + u - 8$ is a polynomial
in the variable $u$ of degree $6$. Expressions like $\frac{1}{x-1} \cdot \sqrt{x} + 2$, $\frac{1}{x^2 + 2x + 3}$ etc., are
not polynomials.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A polynomial of degree 1 is called a **linear polynomial**. For example, $2x - 3$,
$\sqrt{3}x + 5$, $y + \sqrt{2}$, $x - \frac{2}{11}, 3z + 4$, $\frac{2}{3}u + 1$, etc., are all linear polynomials. Polynomials
such as $2x + 5 - x^2$, $x^3 + 1$, etc., are not linear polynomials.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A polynomial of degree 2 is called a \textbf{quadratic polynomial}. The name 'quadratic'
has been derived from the word 'quadrate', which means 'square'. $2x^2 + 3x - \frac{2}{5}$
$y^2 - 2$, $2 - x^2 + \sqrt{3}x$, $\frac{u}{3} - 2u^2 + 5$, $\sqrt{5}v^2 - \frac{2}{3}v$, $4z^2 + \frac{1}{7}$ are some examples of
quadratic polynomials (whose coefficients are real numbers). More generally, any
quadratic polynomial in $x$ is of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, $c$ are real numbers
and $a \neq 0$. A polynomial of degree 3 is called a \textbf{cubic polynomial}. Some examples of

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
a cubic polynomial are $2-x^3, x^3, \sqrt{2} x^3, 3-x^2+x^3, 3x^3-2x^2+x-1$. In fact, the most
general form of a cubic polynomial is

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now consider the polynomial $p(x) = x^2 - 3x - 4$. Then, putting $x = 2$ in the
polynomial, we get $p(2) = 2^2 - 3 \times 2 - 4 = - 6$. The value ‘$- 6$’, obtained by replacing
$x$ by $2$ in $x^2 - 3x - 4$, is the value of $x^2 - 3x - 4$ at $x = 2$. Similarly, $p(0)$ is the value of
$p(x)$ at $x = 0$, which is $- 4$.

replacing $x$ by $k$ in $p(x)$, is called the value of $p(x)$ at $x=k$, and is denoted by $p(k)$.

blocks.text:
As $p(-1) = 0$ and $p(4) = 0, -1$ and $4$ are called the zeroes of the quadratic
polynomial $x^2 - 3x - 4$. More generally, a real number $k$ is said to be a zero of a
polynomial $p(x)$, if $p(k) = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already studied in Class IX, how to find the zeroes of a linear
polynomial. For example, if $k$ is a zero of $p(x) = 2x + 3$, then $p(k) = 0$ gives us
$2k + 3 = 0$, i.e., $k = -\frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In general, if $k$ is a zero of $p(x) = ax + b$, then $p(k) = ak + b = 0$, i.e., $k = \frac{-b}{a}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, the zero of the linear polynomial $ax + b$ is $\frac{-b}{a} = \frac{- (\text{Constant term})}{\text{Coefficient of } x}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the zero of a linear polynomial is related to its coefficients. Does this
happen in the case of other polynomials too? For example, are the zeroes of a quadratic
polynomial also related to its coefficients?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will try to answer these questions. We will also study the
division algorithm for polynomials.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.2 Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You know that a real number $k$ is a zero of the polynomial $p(x)$ if $p(k) = 0$. But why
are the zeroes of a polynomial so important? To answer this, first we will see the
geometrical representations of linear and quadratic polynomials and the geometrical
meaning of their zeroes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Consider first a linear polynomial $ax + b$, $a \neq 0$. You have studied in Class IX that the
graph of $y = ax + b$ is a straight line. For example, the graph of $y = 2x + 3$ is a straight
line passing through the points $(-2, -1)$ and $(2, 7)$.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
x -2 2
y = 2x + 3 -1 7

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Fig. 2.1, you can sec
that the graph of $y = 2x + 3$
intersecis the $x$-axis mid-way
between $x = -1$ and $x = -2$,
that is, at the point $\left(\frac{-3}{2}, 0\right)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You also know that the zero of
$2x + 3$ is $-\frac{3}{2}$. Thus, the zero of
the polynomial $2x + 3$ is the
$x$-coordinate of the point where the
graph of $y = 2x + 3$ intersects the
$x$-axis.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, for a linear polynomial $ax + b$, $a \neq 0$, the graph of $y = ax + b$ is a
straight line which intersects the $x$-axis at exactly one point, namely, $\left(\frac{-b}{a}, 0\right)$.
Therefore, the linear polynomial $ax + b$, $a \neq 0$, has exactly one zero, namely, the
$x$-coordinate of the point where the graph of $y = ax + b$ intersects the $x$-axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us look for the geometrical meaning of a zero of a quadratic polynomial.
Consider the quadratic polynomial $x^2 - 3x - 4$. Let us see what the graph* of
$y = x^2 - 3x - 4$ looks like. Let us list a few values of $y = x^2 - 3x - 4$ corresponding to
a few values for $x$ as given in Table 2.1.

blocks.text:

nor is to be evaluated.

If we locate the points listed
above on a graph paper and draw
the graph, it will actually look like
the one given in Fig. 2.2.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In fact, for any quadratic
polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c, a \neq 0$, the
graph of the corresponding
equation $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ has one
of the two shapes either open
upwards like $\bigcup$ or open
downwards like $\bigcap$ depending on
whether $a > 0$ or $a < 0$. (These
curves are called \textbf{parabolas}.)

blocks.label: Paragraph

You can see from Table 2.1
that $-1$ and $4$ are zeroes of the
quadratic polynomial. Also
note from Fig. 2.2 that $-1$ and $4$
are the $x$-coordinates of the points
where the graph of $y = x^2 - 3x - 4$
intersects the $x$-axis. Thus, the
zeroes of the quadratic polynomial
$x^2 - 3x - 4$ are $x$-coordinates of
the points where the graph of
$y = x^2 - 3x - 4$ intersects the
$x$-axis.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This fact is true for any quadratic polynomial, i.e., the zeroes of a quadratic
polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$, $a \neq 0$, are precisely the $x$-coordinates of the points where the
parabola representing $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ intersects the $x$-axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From our observation earlier about the shape of the graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, the
following three cases can happen:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Case (i) : Here, the graph cuts $x$-axis at two distinct points A and A'.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The $x$-coordinates of A and A' are the two zeroes of the quadratic polynomial
$ax^2 + bx + c$ in this case (see Fig. 2.3).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case (ii) : Here, the graph cuts the $x$-axis at exactly one point, i.e., at two coincident
points. So, the two points $A$ and $A'$ of Case (i) coincide here to become one point $A$
(see Fig. 2.4).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.4

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The $x$-coordinate of A is the only zero for the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$
in this case.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case (iii) : Here, the graph is either completely above the $x$-axis or completely below
the $x$-axis. So, it does not cut the $x$-axis at any point (see Fig. 2.5).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 2.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$ has no zero in this case.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, you can see geometrically that a quadratic polynomial can have either two
distinct zeroes or two equal zeroes (i.e., one zero), or no zero. This also means that a
polynomial of degree 2 has atmost two zeroes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, what do you expect the geometrical meaning of the zeroes of a cubic
polynomial to be? Let us find out. Consider the cubic polynomial $x^3 - 4x$. To see what
the graph of $y = x^3 - 4x$ looks like, let us list a few values of $y$ corresponding to a few
values for $x$ as shown in Table 2.2.

that $- 2, 0$ and $2$ are zeroes of the

that $-2, 0$ and $2$ are, in fact, the

intersects the $x$-axis. Since the curve
meets the $x$-axis in only these $3$

Let us take a few more
examples. Consider the cubic
polynomials $x^3$ and $x^3 - x^2$. We draw
the graphs of $y = x^3$ and $y = x^3 - x^2$
in Fig. 2.7 and Fig. 2.8 respectively.

Note that $0$ is the only zero of the polynomial $x^3$. Also, from Fig. 2.7, you can see
that $0$ is the $x$-coordinate of the only point where the graph of $y = x^3$ intersects the
$x$-axis. Similarly, since $x^3 - x^2 = x^2(x-1)$, $0$ and $1$ are the only zeroes of the polynomial
$x^3 - x^2$. Also, from Fig. 2.8, these values are the $x$-coordinates of the only points
where the graph of $y = x^3 - x^2$ intersects the $x$-axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the examples above, we see that there are at most 3 zeroes for any cubic
polynomial. In other words, any polynomial of degree 3 can have at most three zeroes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : In general, given a polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $n$, the graph of $y = p(x)$
intersects the $x$-axis at atmost $n$ points. Therefore, a polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $n$ has
at most $n$ zeroes.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.3 Relationship between Zeroes and Coefficients of a Polynomial

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already seen that zero of a linear polynomial $ax + b$ is $-\frac{b}{a}$. We will now try
to answer the question raised in Section 2.1 regarding the relationship between zeroes
and coefficients of a quadratic polynomial. For this, let us take a quadratic polynomial,
say $p(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 6$. In Class IX, you have learnt how to factorise quadratic
polynomials by splitting the middle term. So, here we need to split the middle term
‘$- 8x$’ as a sum of two terms, whose product is $6 \times 2x^2 = 12x^2$. So, we write

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the value of $p(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 6$ is zero when $x - 1 = 0$ or $x - 3 = 0$, i.e., when
$x = 1$ or $x = 3$. So, the zeroes of $2x^2 - 8x + 6$ are $1$ and $3$. Observe that :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{Sum of its zeroes} = 1 + 3 = 4 = \frac{-(-8)}{2} = \frac{-(\text{Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Product of its zeroes $= 1 \times 3 = 3 = \frac{6}{2} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take one more quadratic polynomial, say, $p(x) = 3x^2 + 5x - 2$. By the
method of splitting the middle term.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Hence, the value of $3x^2 + 5x - 2$ is zero when either $3x - 1 = 0$ or $x + 2 = 0$, i.e.,
when $x = \frac{1}{3}$ or $x = -2$. So, the zeroes of $3x^2 + 5x - 2$ are $\frac{1}{3}$ and $- 2$. Observe that :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Sum of its zeroes $= \frac{1}{3} + (-2) = \frac{-5}{3} = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Product of its zeroes $= \frac{1}{3} \times (-2) = \frac{-2}{3} =$ Constant term
Coefficient of $x^2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, if $\alpha^*$ and $\beta^*$ are the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$,
$a \neq 0$, then you know that $x - \alpha$ and $x - \beta$ are the factors of $p(x)$. Therefore,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\alpha x^2 + bx + c = k(x - \alpha) (x - \beta)$, where $k$ is a constant
$= k[x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha \cdot \beta]$
$= kx^2 - k(\alpha + \beta)x + k \alpha \beta$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Comparing the coefficients of $x^2$, $x$ and constant terms on both the sides, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$a = k, b = -k(\alpha + \beta) \text{ and } c = k\alpha\beta.$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $\alpha + \beta = \frac{-b}{a}$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}$$

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text:
* $\alpha, \beta$ are Greek letters pronounced as 'alpha' and 'beta' respectively. We will use later one
more letter '$\gamma$' pronounced as 'gamma'.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., sum of zeroes = $\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a} = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: product of zeroes $= \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Find the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $x^2 + 7x + 10$, and verify the
relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.
Solution : We have
$$x^2 + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5)$$
So, the value of $x^2 + 7x + 10$ is zero when $x + 2 = 0$ or $x + 5 = 0$, i.e., when $x = -2$ or
$x = -5$. Therefore, the zeroes of $x^2 + 7x + 10$ are $- 2$ and $- 5$. Now,
$$\text{sum of zeroes} = -2 + (-5) = -(7) = \frac{-(7)}{1} = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2},$$
product of zeroes $= (-2) \times (-5) = 10 = \frac{10}{1} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Find the zeroes of the polynomial $x^2 - 3$ and verify the relationship
between the zeroes and the coefficients.
Solution : Recall the identity $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$. Using it, we can write:
$$x^2 - 3 = (x - \sqrt{3})(x + \sqrt{3})$$
So, the value of $x^2 - 3$ is zero when $x = \sqrt{3}$ or $x = -\sqrt{3}$.
Therefore, the zeroes of $x^2 - 3$ are $\sqrt{3}$ and $-\sqrt{3}$.
Now,
$$\text{sum of zeroes} = \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} = 0 = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2},$$
product of zeroes = $(\sqrt{3})(-\sqrt{3}) = -3 = \frac{-3}{1} = \frac{\text{Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^2}$

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : Find a quadratic polynomial, the sum and product of whose zeroes are
$-3$ and $2$, respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let the quadratic polynomial be $ax^2 + bx + c$, and its zeroes be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \alpha + \beta = -3 = \frac{-b}{a}, $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\alpha\beta = 2 = \frac{c}{a}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If $a = 1$, then $b = 3$ and $c = 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, one quadratic polynomial which fits the given conditions is $x^2 + 3x + 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can check that any other quadratic polynomial that fits these conditions will
be of the form $k(x^2 + 3x + 2)$, where $k$ is real.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now look at cubic polynomials. Do you think a similar relation holds
between the zeroes of a cubic polynomial and its coefficients?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider $p(x) = 2x^3 - 5x^2 - 14x + 8$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can check that $p(x) = 0$ for $x = 4, -2, \frac{1}{2}$. Since $p(x)$ can have atmost three
zeroes, these are the zeroes of $2x^3 - 5x^2 - 14x + 8$. Now,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: sum of the zeroes $= 4 + (-2) + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2} = \frac{-(-5)}{2} = \frac{-\text{(Coefficient of } x^2)}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: product of the zeroes $= 4 \times (-2) \times \frac{1}{2} = -4 = \frac{-8}{2} = \frac{\text{-Constant term}}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
However, there is one more relationship here. Consider the sum of the products
of the zeroes taken two at a time. We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$= -8 - 1 + 2 = -7 = \frac{-14}{2} = \frac{\text{Coefficient of } x}{\text{Coefficient of } x^3}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, it can be proved that if $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the zeroes of the cubic polynomial
$ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = \frac{-b}{a}, $$
$$ \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}, $$
$$ \alpha \beta \gamma = \frac{-d}{a}. $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider an example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5* : Verify that $3, -1, \frac{1}{3}$ are the zeroes of the cubic polynomial
$p(x) = 3x^3 - 5x^2 - 11x - 3$, and then verify the relationship between the zeroes and the
coefficients.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Comparing the given polynomial with $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $3$, $-1$ and $-\frac{1}{3}$ are the zeroes of $3x^3 - 5x^2 - 11x - 3$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we take $\alpha = 3$, $\beta = -1$ and $\gamma = -\frac{1}{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = 3 + (-1) + \left( -\frac{1}{3} \right) = 2 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{3} = \frac{-(-5)}{3} = \frac{-b}{a}, $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha = 3 \times (-1) + (-1) \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) + \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) \times 3 = -3 + \frac{1}{3} - 1 = \frac{-11}{3} = \frac{c}{a},$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\alpha\beta\gamma = 3 \times (-1) \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = 1 = \frac{-(-3)}{3} = \frac{-d}{a}.$$

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * Not from the examination point of view.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.4 Division Algorithm for Polynomials

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You know that a cubic polynomial has at most three zeroes. However, if you are given
only one zero, can you find the other two? For this, let us consider the cubic polynomial
$x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 3$. If we tell you that one of its zeroes is $1$, then you know that $x - 1$ is
a factor of $x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 3$. So, you can divide $x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 3$ by $x - 1$, as you have
learnt in Class IX, to get the quotient $x^2 - 2x - 3$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Next, you could get the factors of $x^2 - 2x - 3$, by splitting the middle term, as
$(x + 1)(x - 3)$. This would give you

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, all the three zeroes of the cubic polynomial are now known to you as
$1, -1, 3.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us discuss the method of dividing one polynomial by another in some detail.
Before noting the steps formally, consider an example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : Divide $2x^2 + 3x + 1$ by $x + 2$.
Solution : Note that we stop the division process when
either the remainder is zero or its degree is less than the
degree of the divisor. So, here the quotient is $2x - 1$ and
the remainder is $3$. Also,

$$
\begin{array}{r}
2x - 1 \\
x + 2 \overline{) 2x^2 + 3x + 1} \\
\underline{2x^2 + 4x} \\
- x + 1 \\
\underline{- x - 2} \\
+ x + \\
\hline
3
\end{array}
$$

(2x - 1)(x + 2) + 3 = 2x^2 + 3x - 2 + 3 = 2x^2 + 3x + 1
i.e., \quad 2x^2 + 3x + 1 = (x + 2)(2x - 1) + 3

Therefore, Dividend = Divisor $\times$ Quotient + Remainder

Let us now extend this process to divide a polynomial by a quadratic polynomial.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : Divide $3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5$ by $1 + 2x + x^2$.

Solution : We first arrange the terms of the dividend and the divisor in the decreasing order of their degrees. Recall that arranging the terms in this order is called writing the polynomials in standard form. In this example, the dividend is already in standard form, and the divisor, in standard form, is $x^2 + 2x + 1$.

$$
\begin{array}{r@{\quad}l}
3x - 5 \\
x^2 + 2x + 1 \overline{) 3x^2 + x^2 + 2x + 5} \\
\underline{3x^3 + 6x^2 + 3x \phantom{{} + 5}} \\
-5x^2 - x + 5 \\
\underline{-5x^2 - 10x - 5} \\
+ \quad + \quad + \\
\hline
9x + 10
\end{array}
$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 1 : To obtain the first term of the quotient, divide the highest degree term of the
dividend (i.e., $3x^3$) by the highest degree term of the divisor (i.e., $x^2$). This is $3x$. Then
carry out the division process. What remains is $-5x^2 - x + 5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 2 : Now, to obtain the second term of the quotient, divide the highest degree term
of the new dividend (i.e., $-5x^2$) by the highest degree term of the divisor (i.e., $x^2$). This
gives $-5$. Again carry out the division process with $-5x^2 - x + 5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 3 : What remains is $9x + 10$. Now, the degree of $9x + 10$ is less than the degree
of the divisor $x^2 + 2x + 1$. So, we cannot continue the division any further.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the quotient is $3x - 5$ and the remainder is $9x + 10$. Also,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here again, we see that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{Dividend} = \text{Divisor} \times \text{Quotient} + \text{Remainder}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What we are applying here is an algorithm which is similar to Euclid's division
algorithm that you studied in Chapter 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This says that

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $p(x)$ and $g(x)$ are any two polynomials with $g(x) \neq 0$, then we can find
polynomials $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ such that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$p(x) = g(x) \times q(x) + r(x),$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where $r(x) = 0$ or degree of $r(x) <$ degree of $g(x)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This result is known as the Division Algorithm for polynomials.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us now take some examples to illustrate its use.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 8 : Divide $3x^2 - x^3 - 3x + 5$ by $x - 1 - x^2$, and verify the division algorithm.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: POLYNOMIALS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Note that the given polynomials
are not in standard form. To carry out
division, we first write both the dividend and
divisor in decreasing orders of their degrees.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$
\begin{array}{r@{\quad}l}
x - 2 \\
-x^2 + x - 1 \overline{) -x^3 + 3x^2 - 3x + 5} \\
\underline{-x^3 + \phantom{3}x^2 - \phantom{3}x} \\
\underline{- \phantom{3} + \phantom{3} + \phantom{3} +} \\
2x^2 - 2x + 5 \\
\underline{2x^2 - 2x + 2} \\
- \phantom{2} + \phantom{2} - \\
\hline
\phantom{-x^3 + 3x^2 - 3x +} 3
\end{array}
$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, dividend $= -x^3 + 3x^2 - 3x + 5$ and
divisor $= -x^2 + x - 1.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Division process is shown on the right side.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We stop here since degree $(3) = 0 < 2 =$ degree $(-x^2 + x - 1)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, quotient $= x - 2$, remainder $= 3$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Divisor $\times$ Quotient + Remainder
$= (-x^2 + x - 1) (x - 2) + 3$
$= -x^3 + x^2 - x + 2x^2 - 2x + 2 + 3$
$= -x^3 + 3x^2 - 3x + 5$
$= \text{Dividend}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this way, the division algorithm is verified.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 : Find all the zeroes of $2x^4 - 3x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 2$, if you know that two of
its zeroes are $\sqrt{2}$ and $-\sqrt{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Since two zeroes are $\sqrt{2}$ and $-\sqrt{2}$. $(x-\sqrt{2})(x+\sqrt{2}) = x^2 - 2$ is a
factor of the given polynomial. Now, we divide the given polynomial by $x^2 - 2$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{}} 2x^3 - 3x + 1 \\
x^2 - 2 \overline{) 2x^4 - 3x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 2} \\
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{}} \underline{- 2x^4 \phantom{- 3x^3} - 4x^2} \\
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{}} - 3x^3 + x^3 + 6x - 2 \\
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{}} \underline{- 3x^3 \phantom{{}+ x^3} + 6x} \\
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{ - 3x^3 + } } x^2 \phantom{{}+ 6x} - 2 \\
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{ - 3x^3 + } } \underline{- \phantom{3} x^2 \phantom{{}+ 6x} - 2} \\
\phantom{x^2 - 2 \sqrt{ - 3x^3 + x^3 + } - 3x^2} 0
\end{array}
$$

First term of quotient is $\frac{2x^4}{x^2} = 2x^2$

Second term of quotient is $\frac{-3x^3}{x^2} = -3x$

Third term of quotient is $\frac{x^2}{x^2} = 1$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, by splitting $-3x$, we factorise $2x^2 - 3x + 1$ as $(2x - 1)(x - 1)$. So, its zeroes
are given by $x = \frac{1}{2}$ and $x = 1$. Therefore, the zeroes of the given polynomial are
$\sqrt{2}$, $-\sqrt{2}$, $\frac{1}{2}$, and $1$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 2.5 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Polynomials of degrees 1, 2 and 3 are called linear, quadratic and cubic polynomials
respectively.
2. A quadratic polynomial in $x$ with real coefficients is of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a, b, c$
are real numbers with $a \neq 0$.
3. The zeroes of a polynomial $p(x)$ are precisely the $x$-coordinates of the points, where the
graph of $y = p(x)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
4. A quadratic polynomial can have at most 2 zeroes and a cubic polynomial can have
at most 3 zeroes.
5. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial $ax^2 + bx + c$, then

$$ \alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}, \quad \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}. $$

6. If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the zeroes of the cubic polynomial $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$, then

$$ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = \frac{-b}{a}, $$

$$ \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}. $$

and $\alpha\beta\gamma = \frac{-d}{a}$.

7. The division algorithm states that given any polynomial $p(x)$ and any non-zero
polynomial $g(x)$, there are polynomials $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ such that

$$ p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x), $$

where $r(x) = 0$ or degree $r(x) <$ degree $g(x)$.

PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS
IN TWO VARIABLES 3

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: You must have come across situations like the one given below :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Akhila went to a fair in her village. She wanted to enjoy rides on the Giant Wheel
and play Hoopla (a game in which you throw a ring on the items kept in a stall, and if
the ring covers any object completely, you get it). The number of times she played
Hoopla is half the number of rides she had on the Giant Wheel. If each ride costs
Rs 3, and a game of Hoopla costs Rs 4, how would you find out the number of rides
she had and how many times she played Hoopla, provided she spent Rs 20.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
May be you will try it by considering different cases. If she has one ride, is it
possible? Is it possible to have two rides? And so on. Or you may use the knowledge
of Class IX, to represent such situations as linear equations in two variables.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us try this approach.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Denote the number of rides that Akhila had by $x$, and the number of times she
played Hoopla by $y$. Now the situation can be represented by the two equations:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$y = \frac{1}{2}x \qquad (1)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Can we find the solutions of this pair of equations? There are several ways of
finding these, which we will study in this chapter.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.2 Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall, from Class IX, that the following are examples of linear equations in two
variables:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You also know that an equation which can be put in the form $ax + by + c = 0$,
where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are real numbers, and $a$ and $b$ are **not both zero**, is called a linear
equation in two variables $x$ and $y$. (We often denote the condition $a$ and $b$ are not both
zero by $a^2 + b^2 \neq 0$). You have also studied that a solution of such an equation is a
pair of values, one for $x$ and the other for $y$, which makes the two sides of the
equation equal.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For example, let us substitute $x = 1$ and $y = 1$ in the left hand side (LHS) of the
equation $2x + 3y = 5$. Then

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is equal to the right hand side (RHS) of the equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $x = 1$ and $y = 1$ is a solution of the equation $2x + 3y = 5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now let us substitute $x = 1$ and $y = 7$ in the equation $2x + 3y = 5$. Then,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is not equal to the RHS.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $x = 1$ and $y = 7$ is not a solution of the equation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Geometrically, what does this mean? It means that the point $(1, 1)$ lies on the line
representing the equation $2x + 3y = 5$, and the point $(1, 7)$ does not lie on it. So, every
solution of the equation is a point on the line representing it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In fact, this is true for any linear equation, that is, each solution $(x, y)$ of a
linear equation in two variables, $ax + by + c = 0$, corresponds to a point on the
line representing the equation, and vice versa.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, consider Equations (1) and (2) given above. These equations, taken
together, represent the information we have about Akhila at the fair.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
These two linear equations are in the same two variables $x$ and $y$. Equations
like these are called a pair of linear equations in two variables.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us see what such pairs look like algebraically.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.3 Graphical Method of Solution of a Pair of Linear Equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, you have seen how we can graphically represent a pair of
linear equations as two lines. You have also seen that the lines may intersect, or may
be parallel, or may coincide. Can we solve them in each case? And if so, how? We
shall try and answer these questions from the geometrical point of view in this section.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us look at the earlier examples one by one.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
● In the situation of Example 1, find out how many rides on the Giant Wheel
Akhila had, and how many times she played Hoopla.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 3.2, you noted that the equations representing the situation are
geometrically shown by two lines intersecting at the point $(4, 2)$. Therefore, the

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
point $(4, 2)$ lies on the lines represented by both the equations $x - 2y = 0$ and
$3x + 4y = 20$. And this is the only common point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us verify algebraically that $x = 4$, $y = 2$ is a solution of the given
pair of equations. Substituting the values of $x$ and $y$ in each equation, we get
$4 - 2 \times 2 = 0$ and $3(4) + 4(2) = 20$. So, we have verified that $x = 4$, $y = 2$ is a
solution of both the equations. Since $(4, 2)$ is the only common point on both
the lines, there is one and only one solution for this pair of linear equations
in two variables.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the number of rides Akhila had on Giant Wheel is 4 and the number
of times she played Hoopla is 2.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
• In the situation of Example 2, can you find the cost of each pencil and each
eraser?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 3.3, the situation is geometrically shown by a pair of coincident
lines. The solutions of the equations are given by the common points.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Are there any common points on these lines? From the graph, we observe
that every point on the line is a common solution to both the equations. So, the
equations $2x + 3y = 9$ and $4x + 6y = 18$ have infinitely many solutions. This
should not surprise us, because if we divide the equation $4x + 6y = 18$ by $2$ , we
get $2x + 3y = 9$, which is the same as Equation (1). That is, both the equations are
equivalent. From the graph, we see that any point on the line gives us a possible
cost of each pencil and eraser. For instance, each pencil and eraser can cost
$ \text{\`} 3 \text{ and } \text{\`} 1 \text{ respectively. Or, each pencil can cost } \text{\`} 3.75 \text{ and eraser can cost } $ $ $ 0.50, \text{ and so on.} $

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: • In the situation of Example 3, can the two rails cross each other?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 3.4, the situation is represented geometrically by two parallel lines.
Since the lines do not intersect at all, the rails do not cross. This also means that
the equations have no common solution.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A pair of linear equations which has no solution, is called an inconsistent pair of
linear equations. A pair of linear equations in two variables, which has a solution, is
called a consistent pair of linear equations. A pair of linear equations which are
equivalent has infinitely many distinct common solutions. Such a pair is called a
dependent pair of linear equations in two variables. Note that a dependent pair of
linear equations is always consistent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can now summarise the behaviour of lines representing a pair of linear equations
in two variables and the existence of solutions as follows:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) the lines may intersect in a single point. In this case, the pair of equations
has a unique solution (consistent pair of equations).

(ii) the lines may be parallel. In this case, the equations have no solution
(inconsistent pair of equations).

(iii) the lines may be coincident. In this case, the equations have infinitely many
solutions [dependent (consistent) pair of equations].

blocks.text:

(iii) $x + 2y - 4 = 0$ and $2x + 4y - 12 = 0$      (The lines are parallel)

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.4 Algebraic Methods of Solving a Pair of Linear Equations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, we discussed how to solve a pair of linear equations graphically.
The graphical method is not convenient in cases when the point representing the
solution of the linear equations has non-integral coordinates like $\left(\sqrt{3}, 2\sqrt{7}\right)$,
$(-1.75, 3.3)$, $\left(\frac{4}{13}, \frac{1}{19}\right)$, etc. There is every possibility of making mistakes while reading
such coordinates. Is there any alternative method of finding the solution? There are
several algebraic methods, which we shall now discuss.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
3.4.1 Substitution Method : We shall explain the method of substitution by taking
some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To understand the substitution method more clearly, let us consider it stepwise:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 1 : Find the value of one variable, say $y$ in terms of the other variable, i.e., $x$ from
either equation, whichever is convenient.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 2 : Substitute this value of $y$ in the other equation, and reduce it to an equation in
one variable, i.e., in terms of $x$, which can be solved. Sometimes, as in Examples 9 and
10 below, you can get statements with no variable. If this statement is true, you can
conclude that the pair of linear equations has infinitely many solutions. If the statement
is false, then the pair of linear equations is inconsistent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 3 : Substitute the value of $x$ (or $y$) obtained in Step 2 in the equation used in
Step 1 to obtain the value of the other variable.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\underline{Remark} : We have \textbf{substituted} the value of one variable by expressing it in terms of
the other variable to solve the pair of linear equations. That is why the method is
known as the \textit{substitution method}.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. The method used in solving the example above is called the elimination method,
because we eliminate one variable first, to get a linear equation in one variable.
In the example above, we eliminated $y$. We could also have eliminated $x$. Try
doing it that way.
2. You could also have used the substitution, or graphical method, to solve this
problem. Try doing so, and see which method is more convenient.
Let us now note down these steps in the elimination method :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 1 : First multiply both the equations by some suitable non-zero constants to make
the coefficients of one variable (either $x$ or $y$) numerically equal.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 2 : Then add or subtract one equation from the other so that one variable gets
eliminated. If you get an equation in one variable, go to Step 3.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If in Step 2, we obtain a true statement involving no variable, then the original
pair of equations has infinitely many solutions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If in Step 2, we obtain a false statement involving no variable, then the original
pair of equations has no solution, i.e., it is inconsistent.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Step 3 : Solve the equation in one variable ($x$ or $y$) so obtained to get its value.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Step 4 : Substitute this value of $x$ (or $y$) in either of the original equations to get the
value of the other variable.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now to illustrate it, we shall solve few more examples.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 3.6 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Two linear equations in the same two variables are called a pair of linear equations in two
variables. The most general form of a pair of linear equations is
$$a_1^2x + b_1y + c_1 = 0$$
$$a_2^2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0$$
where $a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2, c_1, c_2$ are real numbers, such that $a_1^2 + b_1^2 \neq 0, a_2^2 + b_2^2 \neq 0$.
2. A pair of linear equations in two variables can be represented, and solved, by the:
(i) graphical method
(ii) algebraic method
3. Graphical Method :
The graph of a pair of linear equations in two variables is represented by two lines.
(i) If the lines intersect at a point, then that point gives the unique solution of the two
equations. In this case, the pair of equations is consistent.
(ii) If the lines coincide, then there are infinitely many solutions — each point on the
line being a solution. In this case, the pair of equations is dependent (consistent).
(iii) If the lines are parallel, then the pair of equations has no solution. In this case, the
pair of equations is inconsistent.
4. Algebraic Methods : We have discussed the following methods for finding the solution(s)
of a pair of linear equations :
(i) Substitution Method
(ii) Elimination Method
(iii) Cross-multiplication Method
5. If a pair of linear equations is given by $a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0$, then the
following situations can arise :
(i) $\frac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \frac{b_1}{b_1}$ : In this case, the pair of linear equations is consistent.
(ii) $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \frac{c_1}{c_2}$ : In this case, the pair of linear equations is inconsistent.
(iii) $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{c_1}{c_2}$ : In this case, the pair of linear equations is dependent and consistent.
6. There are several situations which can be mathematically represented by two equations
that are not linear to start with. But we alter them so that they are reduced to a pair of
linear equations.
