\underline{Example 1} : Do the points $(3, 2)$, $(-2, -3)$ and $(2, 3)$ form a triangle? If so, name the
type of triangle formed.

\underline{Solution} : Let us apply the distance formula to find the distances $PQ$, $QR$ and $PR$,
where $P(3, 2)$, $Q(-2, -3)$ and $R(2, 3)$ are the given points. We have

$$PQ = \sqrt{(3+2)^2 + (2+3)^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{50} = 7.07 \text{ (approx.)}$$

$$QR = \sqrt{(-2-2)^2 + (-3-3)^2} = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-6)^2} = \sqrt{52} = 7.21 \text{ (approx.)}$$

$$PR = \sqrt{(3-2)^2 + (2-3)^2} = \sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2} = 1.41 \text{ (approx.)}$$

Since the sum of any two of these distances is greater than the third distance, therefore,
the points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ form a triangle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since the sum of any two of these distances is greater than the third distance, therefore,
the points P, Q and R form a triangle.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: COORDINATE GEOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also, $PQ^2 + PR^2 = QR^2$, by the converse of Pythagoras theorem, we have $\angle P = 90^\circ$.
Therefore, PQR is a right triangle.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 2} : Show that the points $(1, 7), (4, 2), (-1, -1)$ and $(- 4, 4)$ are the vertices
of a square.

\underline{Solution} : Let $A(1, 7), B(4, 2), C(-1, -1)$ and $D(- 4, 4)$ be the given points. One way
of showing that ABCD is a square is to use the property that all its sides should be
equal and both its diagonals should also be equal. Now,

$$AB = \sqrt{(1 - 4)^2 + (7 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$BC = \sqrt{(4 + 1)^2 + (2 + 1)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$CD = \sqrt{(-1 + 4)^2 + (-1 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$DA = \sqrt{(1 + 4)^2 + (7 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$AC = \sqrt{(1 + 1)^2 + (7 + 1)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 64} = \sqrt{68}$$
$$BD = \sqrt{(4 + 4)^2 + (2 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{64 + 4} = \sqrt{68}$$

Since, $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $AC = BD$, all the four sides of the quadrilateral
ABCD are equal and its diagonals AC and BD are also equal. Thereore, ABCD is a
square.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since, $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $AC = BD$, all the four sides of the quadrilateral
$ABCD$ are equal and its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are also equal. Thereore, $ABCD$ is a
square.

the converse of Pythagoras
theorem, $\angle D = 90^\circ$. A quadrilateral
with all four sides equal and one
angle $90^\circ$ is a square. So, ABCD
is a square.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 7.3 Section Formula

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us recall the situation in Section 7.2.
Suppose a telephone company wants to
position a relay tower at P between A and B
is such a way that the distance of the tower
from B is twice its distance from A. If P lies
on AB, it will divide AB in the ratio $1 : 2$
(see Fig. 7.9). If we take A as the origin O,
and 1 km as one unit on both the axis, the
coordinates of B will be $(36, 15)$. In order to
know the position of the tower, we must know
the coordinates of P. How do we find these
coordinates?

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 7.9

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let the coordinates of P be $(x, y)$. Draw perpendiculars from P and B to the
$x$-axis, meeting it in D and E, respectively. Draw PC perpendicular to BE. Then, by
the AA similarity criterion, studied in Chapter 6, $\Delta$ POD and $\Delta$ BPC are similar.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore , $\frac{\text{OD}}{\text{PC}} = \frac{\text{OP}}{\text{PB}} = \frac{1}{2}$, and $\frac{\text{PD}}{\text{BC}} = \frac{\text{OP}}{\text{PB}} = \frac{1}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{x}{36-x} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{y}{15-y} = \frac{1}{2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: These equations give $x = 12$ and $y = 5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can check that $P(12, 5)$ meets the
condition that $OP : PB = 1 : 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now let us use the understanding that
you may have developed through this
example to obtain the general formula.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Consider any two points $A(x_1, y_1)$ and
$B(x_2, y_2)$ and assume that $P(x, y)$ divides
AB internally in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$, i.e.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{PA}{PB} = \frac{m_1}{m_2} \text{ (see Fig. 7.10).} $$

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: COORDINATE GEOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw AR, PS and BT perpendicular to the $x$-axis. Draw AQ and PC parallel to
the $x$-axis. Then, by the AA similarity criterion,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\Delta$ PAQ - $\Delta$ BPC

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{PA}{BP} = \frac{AQ}{PC} = \frac{PQ}{BC}$ (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\mathrm{AQ} = \mathrm{RS} = \mathrm{OS} - \mathrm{OR} = x - x_1$
$\mathrm{PC} = \mathrm{ST} = \mathrm{OT} - \mathrm{OS} = x_2 - x$
$\mathrm{PQ} = \mathrm{PS} - \mathrm{QS} = \mathrm{PS} - \mathrm{AR} = y - y_1$
$\mathrm{BC} = \mathrm{BT} - \mathrm{CT} = \mathrm{BT} - \mathrm{PS} = y_2 - y$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting these values in (1), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Taking $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x}$, we get $x = \frac{m_1 x_2 + m_2 x_1}{m_1 + m_2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, taking $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{y - y_1}{y_2 - y}$, we get $y = \frac{m_1 y_2 + m_2 y_1}{m_1 + m_2}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the coordinates of the point P$(x, y)$ which divides the line segment joining the
points A$(x_1, y_1)$ and B$(x_2, y_2)$, internally, in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ are

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This is known as the section formula.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This can also be derived by drawing perpendiculars from A, P and B on the
y-axis and proceeding as above.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If the ratio in which $\bar{\mathrm{P}}$ divides $\mathrm{AB}$ is $k : 1$, then the coordinates of the point $\mathrm{P}$ will be

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{kx_2 + x_1}{k+1} , \frac{ky_2 + y_1}{k+1} \right) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Special Case : The mid-point of a line segment divides the line segment in the ratio
$1 : 1$. Therefore, the coordinates of the mid-point P of the join of the points $A(x_1, y_1)$
and $B(x_2, y_2)$ is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{1 \cdot x_1 + 1 \cdot x_2}{1 + 1}, \frac{1 \cdot y_1 + 1 \cdot y_2}{1 + 1} \right) = \left( \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right). $$

parallelogram, taken in order, find the value of $p$.

\underline{\text{Solution}} : We know that diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

So, the coordinates of the mid-point of AC = coordinates of the mid-point of BD

i.e., $\left(\frac{6+9}{2}, \frac{1+4}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{8+p}{2}, \frac{2+3}{2}\right)$

i.e., $\left(\frac{15}{2}, \frac{5}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{8+p}{2}, \frac{5}{2}\right)$

so, $\frac{15}{2} = \frac{8+p}{2}$

i.e., $p = 7$

Section 7.3 discusses the Section Formula for the coordinates $(x, y)$ of a
point P which divides internally the line segment joining the points

externally the line segment joining the points A and B. You will study

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In all the situations given above, the distances or heights can be found by using
some mathematical techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called
'trigonometry'. The word 'trigonometry' is derived from the Greek words 'tri'
(meaning three), 'gon' (meaning sides) and 'metron' (meaning measure). In fact,
trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and Babylon. Early
astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets from the Earth.
Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in Engineering and
Physical Sciences are based on trigonometrical concepts.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with
respect to its acute angles, called **trigonometric ratios of the angle**. We will restrict
our discussion to acute angles only. However, these ratios can be extended to other
angles also. We will also define the trigonometric ratios for angles of measure $0^\circ$ and
$90^\circ$. We will calculate trigonometric ratios for some specific angles and establish
some identities involving these ratios, called **trigonometric identities**.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.2 Trigonometric Ratios

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Section 8.1, you have seen some right triangles
imagined to be formed in different situations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take a right triangle ABC as shown
in Fig. 8.4.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, $\angle CAB$ (or, in brief, angle A) is an
acute angle. Note the position of the side BC
with respect to angle A. It faces $\angle A$. We call it
the side opposite to angle A. AC is the
hypotenuse of the right triangle and the side AB
is a part of $\angle A$. So, we call it the side
adjacent to angle A.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.4

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that the position of sides change
when you consider angle C in place of A
(see Fig. 8.5).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have studied the concept of 'ratio' in
your earlier classes. We now define certain ratios
involving the sides of a right triangle, and call
them trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The trigonometric ratios of the angle A
in right triangle ABC (see Fig. 8.4) are defined
as follows :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{sine of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{BC}{AC} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{cosine of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{AB}{AC} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: tangent of $\angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{BC}{AB}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$cosecant of \angle A = \frac{1}{\sin\epsilon\text{ of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{AC}{BC}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$secant \ of \ \angle A = \frac{1}{\cosine \ of \ \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side adjacent to angle } A} = \frac{AC}{AB}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: cotangent of $\angle A = \frac{1}{\text{tangent of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{AB}{BC}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The ratios defined above are abbreviated as $\sin A$, $\cos A$, $\tan A$, $\csc A$, $\sec A$
and $\cot A$ respectively. Note that the ratios $\mathbf{cosec A}$, $\mathbf{sec A}$ and $\cot A$ are respectively,
the reciprocals of the ratios $\sin A$, $\cos A$ and $\tan A$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, observe that $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{\frac{BC}{AC}}{\frac{AB}{AC}} = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}$ and $\cot A = \frac{\cos A}{\sin A}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle express the
relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Why don't you try to define the trigonometric ratios for angle C in the right
triangle? (See Fig. 8.5)

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
The first use of the idea of ‘sine’ in the way we use
it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata,
in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardhā-jya
for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or
jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was
translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as
it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which
means curve, when the Arabic version was translated
into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine,
became common in mathematical texts throughout
Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund
Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated
notation ‘sin’.

The origin of the terms ‘cosine’ and ‘tangent’ was much later. The cosine function
arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta
called it kotijya. The name cosinus originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the
English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation ‘eos’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Note that the symbol $\sin A$ is used as an
abbreviation for 'the sine of the angle A', $\sin A$ is not
the product of '$\sin$' and A. '$\sin$' separated from A
has no meaning. Similarly, $\cos A$ is not the product of
'$\cos$' and A. Similar interpretations follow for other
trigonometric ratios also.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse
AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle
ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN
perpendicular to AB extended (see Fig. 8.6), how
will the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ PAM differ
from those of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ CAB or from those of $\angle A$ in
$\Delta$ QAN?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To answer this, first look at these triangles. Is $\Delta$ PAM similar to $\Delta$ CAB? From
Chapter 6, recall the AA similarity criterion. Using the criterion, you will see that the
triangles PAM and CAB are similar. Therefore, by the property of similar triangles,
the corresponding sides of the triangles are proportional.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we have $\frac{AM}{AB} = \frac{AP}{AC} = \frac{MP}{BC}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: From this, we find $\frac{MP}{AP} = \frac{BC}{AC} = \sin A$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, $\frac{AM}{AP} = \frac{AB}{AC} = \cos A$, $\frac{MP}{AM} = \frac{BC}{AB} = \tan A$ and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This shows that the trigonometric ratios of angle A in $\Delta$ PAM not differ from
those of angle $\Lambda$ in $\Delta$ CAB.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the same way, you should check that the value of $\sin \Delta$ (and also of other
trigonometric ratios) remains the same in $\Delta$ QAN also.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric
ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if
the angle remains the same.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** For the sake of convenience, we may write $\sin^{-2}A$, $\cos^{-2}A$, etc., in place of
$(\sin A)^2$, $(\cos A)^2$, etc., respectively. But $\csc A = (\sin A)^{-1} \neq \sin^{-1} A$ (it is called sine
inverse A). $\sin^{-1} A$ has a different meaning, which will be discussed in higher classes.
Similar conventions hold for the other trigonometric ratios as well. Sometimes, the
Greek letter $\theta$ (theta) is also used to denote an angle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. If we know any one
of the ratios, can we obtain the other ratios? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If in a right triangle ABC, $\sin A = \frac{1}{3}$,
then this means that $\frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{1}{3}$, i.e., the
lengths of the sides BC and AC of the triangle
ABC are in the ratio $1:3$ (see Fig. 8.7). So if
BC is equal to $k$, then AC will be $3k$, where
$k$ is any positive number. To determine other
trigonometric ratios for the angle A, we need to find the length of the third side
AB. Do you remember the Pythagoras theorem? Let us use it to determine the
required length AB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AB = \pm 2\sqrt{2}k$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we get $AB = 2\sqrt{2}k$ (Why is $AB$ not $-2\sqrt{2}k$?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}k}{3k} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Similarly, you can obtain the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of
$\sin A$ or $\cos A$ is always less than $1$ (or, in particular, equal to $1$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Given $\tan A = \frac{4}{3}$, find the other
trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.text:
Solution : Let us first draw a right $\Delta$ ABC
(see Fig 8.8).

Therefore, if BC = $4k$, then AB = $3k$, where $k$ is a
positive number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, by using the Pythagoras Theorem. we have

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we can write all the trigonometric ratios using their definitions.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{4k}{5k} = \frac{4}{5}$$
$$\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{3k}{5k} = \frac{3}{5}$$

\underline{Example 2} : If $\angle B$ and $\angle Q$ are
acute angles such that $\sin B = \sin Q$,
then prove that $\angle B = \angle Q$.

\underline{Solution} : Let us consider two right

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{PR}} = \frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{PQ}} = k$, say (1)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now. using Pythagoras theorem.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$BC = \sqrt{AB^2 - AC^2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $QR = \sqrt{PQ^2 - PR^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QR}}=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{AB}^{2}-\mathrm{AC}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^{2}-\mathrm{PR}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{k}^{2}\mathrm{PQ}^{2}-\mathrm{k}^{2}\mathrm{PR}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^{2}-\mathrm{PR}^{2}}}=\frac{\mathrm{k}\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^{2}-\mathrm{PR}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^{2}-\mathrm{PR}^{2}}}=\mathrm{k}$ (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: From (1) and (2), we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{AC}{PR} = \frac{AB}{PQ} = \frac{BC}{QR} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then, by using Theorem 6.4, $\Delta$ ACB $\sim \Delta$ PRQ and therefore, $\angle \mathrm{B} = \angle \mathrm{Q}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Consider $\Delta$ ACB, right-angled at C, in
which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units and $\angle$ ABC = $\theta$
(see Fig. 8.10). Determine the values of
(i) $\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta$,
(ii) $\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta$.
Solution : In $\Delta$ ACB, we have
$$AC = \sqrt{AB^2 - BC^2} = \sqrt{(29)^2 - (21)^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{(29 - 2J)(29 + 2I)} = \sqrt{(8)(50)} = \sqrt{400} = 20 \text{ units}$$
So, $\sin \theta = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{20}{29}, \cos \theta = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{21}{29}$.
Now, (i) $\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = \left(\frac{20}{29}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{21}{29}\right)^2 = \frac{20^2 + 21^2}{29^2} = \frac{400 + 441}{841} = 1$,
and (ii) $\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta = \left(\frac{21}{29}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{20}{29}\right)^2 = \frac{(21 + 20)(21 - 20)}{29^2} = \frac{41}{841}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
if $\tan A = 1$, then verify that
$2 \sin A \cos A = 1$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Solution : In $\Delta$ ABC, $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = 1$ (see Fig 8.11)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $BC = AB$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let AB = BC = k, where k is a positive number.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $AC = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2}$
$= \sqrt{(k)^2 + (k)^2} = k\sqrt{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $2 \sin A \cos A = 2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 1$, which is the required value.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 5} : In $\Delta$ OPQ, right-angled at P,
OP = 7 cm and OQ – PQ = 1 cm (see Fig. 8.12).
Determine the values of $\sin Q$ and $\cos Q$.

\underline{Solution} : In $\Delta$ OPQ, we have

$$OQ^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2$$

i.e., \qquad $(1 + PQ)^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2$ \qquad (Why?)

i.e., \qquad $1 + PQ^2 + 2PQ = OP^2 + PQ^2$

i.e., \qquad $1 + 2PQ = 7^2$ \qquad \qquad (Why?)

i.e., \qquad $PQ = 24 \text{ cm and } OQ = 1 + PQ = 25 \text{ cm}$

So, \qquad $\sin Q = \frac{7}{25}$ and $\cos Q = \frac{24}{25}$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.3 Trigonometric Ratios of Some Specific Angles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From geometry, you are already familiar with the construction of angles of $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$,
$60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$. In this section, we will find the values of the trigonometric ratios for these
angles and, of course, for $0^\circ$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $45^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is $45^\circ$, then
the other angle is also $45^\circ$, i.e., $\angle A = \angle C = 45^\circ$
(sec Fig. 8.14).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\text{BC} = \text{AB} \quad (\text{Why?})$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, Suppose BC = AB = a.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then by Pythagoras Theorem, $AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and, therefore, $AC = a\sqrt{2}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using the definitions of the trigonometric ratios, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin 45^\circ = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^\circ}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \cos 45^\circ = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^\circ}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \tan 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^{\circ}} = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{a}{a} = 1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $\csc 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 45^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2}$, $\sec 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 45^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2}$, $\cot 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 45^{\circ}} = 1$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now calculate the trigonometric ratios of $30^{\circ}$
and $60^{\circ}$. Consider an equilateral triangle ABC. Since
each angle in an equilateral triangle is $60^{\circ}$, therefore,
$\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = 60^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw the perpendicular AD from A to the side BC
(sec Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now $\Delta ABD \cong \Delta ACD$ (Why?)
Therefore, $BD = DC$
and $\angle BAD = \angle CAD$ (CPCT)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now observe that:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\Delta$ ABD is a right triangle, right-angled at D with $\angle$ BAD $= 30^{\circ}$ and $\angle$ ABD $= 60^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: INTRODUCTION TO TRIGONOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As you know, for finding the trigonometric ratios, we need to know the lengths of the
sides of the triangle. So, let us suppose that $AB = 2a$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then, $BD = \frac{1}{2} BC = a$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AD = a\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
ve :
$\sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{2a} = \frac{1}{2}, \cos 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Also, $\csc 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = 2, \sec 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 30^{\circ}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$
$\cot 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 30^{\circ}} = \sqrt{3}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Similarly,
$\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}, \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3},$
$\csc 60^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \sec 60^{\circ} = 2 \text{ and } \cot 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of angle
A, if it is made smaller and smaller in the right triangle ABC
(see Fig. 8.16), till it becomes zero. As $\angle A$ gets smaller and
smaller, the length of the side BC decreases. The point C gets
closer to point B, and finally when $\angle A$ becomes very close
to $0^{\circ}$, AC becomes almost the same as AB (see Fig. 8.17).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle A$ is very close to $0^\circ$, BC gets very close to $0$ and so the value of
$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}$ is very close to $0$. Also, when $\angle A$ is very close to $0^\circ$, AC is nearly the

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: same as AB and so the value of $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC}$ is very close to 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This helps us to see how we can define the values of $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ when
$A = 0^\circ$. We define : $\sin 0^\circ = 0$ and $\cos 0^\circ = 1$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using these, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\tan 0^{\circ} = \frac{\sin 0^{\circ}}{\cos 0^{\circ}} = 0, \cot 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 0^{\circ}}$, which is not defined. (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\sec 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 0^{\circ}} = 1$ and $\csc 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 0^{\circ}}$, which is again not defined.(Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$, when it is made
larger and larger in $\Delta ABC$ till it becomes $90^\circ$. As $\angle A$ gets larger and larger, $\angle C$ gets
smaller and smaller. Therefore, as in the case above, the length of the side AB goes on
decreasing. The point A gets closer to point B. Finally when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$,
$\angle C$ becomes very close to $0^\circ$ and the side AC almost coincides with side BC
(see Fig. 8.18).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle C$ is very close to $0^\circ$, $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$, side AC is nearly the
same as side BC, and so $\sin A$ is very close to 1. Also when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$,
$\angle C$ is very close to $0^\circ$, and the side AB is nearly zero, so $\cos A$ is very close to 0.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we define: $\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$ and $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, why don't you find the other trigonometric ratios of $90^\circ$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We shall now give the values of all the trigonometric ratios of $0^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$
and $90^\circ$ in Table 8.1, for ready reference.

blocks.label: Table-caption
blocks.text: Table 8.1

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
$\angle A$ $0^\circ$ $30^\circ$ $45^\circ$ $60^\circ$ $90^\circ$
$\sin A$ 0 $\frac{1}{2}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ 1
$\cos A$ 1 $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{1}{2}$ 0
$\tan A$ 0 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1 $\sqrt{3}$ Not defined
$\text{cosec } A$ Not defined 2 $\sqrt{2}$ $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1
$\sec A$ 1 $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\sqrt{2}$ 2 Not defined
$\cot A$ Not defined $\sqrt{3}$ 1 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 0

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\underline{Remark} : From the table above you can observe that as $\angle$ A increases from $0^{\circ}$ to
$90^{\circ}$, $\sin$ A increases from $0$ to $1$ and $\cos$ A decreases from $1$ to $0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us illustrate the use of the values in the table above through some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{Example 6} : In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B,
AB = 5 cm and $\angle ACB = 30^{\circ}$ (see Fig. 8.19).
Determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC.
\textbf{Solution} : To find the length of the side BC, we will
choose the trigonometric ratio involving BC and the
given side AB. Since BC is the side adjacent to angle
C and AB is the side opposite to angle C, therefore

$$ \frac{AB}{BC} = \tan C $$

i.e., $\frac{5}{BC} = \tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

which gives $BC = 5\sqrt{3}$ cm

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To find the length of the side AC, we consider

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{AC} \qquad (\text{Why?}) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $AC = 10 \text{ cm}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that alternatively we could have used Pythagoras theorem to determine the third
side in the example above.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $AC = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2} = \sqrt{s^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2} \text{ cm} = 10\text{cm}.$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : In $\Delta$ PQR, right-angled at
Q (see Fig. 8.20), PQ = 3 cm and PR = 6 cm.
Determine $\angle$ QPR and $\angle$ PRQ.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Given PQ = 3 cm and PR = 6 cm.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{PQ}{PR} = \sin R$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\sin R = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle PRQ = 30^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and therefore, $\angle QPR = 60^\circ$. (Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may note that if one of the sides and any other part (either an acute angle or any
side) of a right triangle is known, the remaining sides and angles of the triangle can be
determined.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 8 : If $\sin (A - B) = \frac{1}{2}$, $\cos (A + B) = \frac{1}{2}$, $0^\circ < A + B \le 90^\circ$, $A > B$, find A
and B.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : Since, $\sin (A - B) = \frac{1}{2}$, therefore, $A - B = 30^\circ$   (Why?)      (1)
Also, since $\cos (A + B) = \frac{1}{2}$, therefore, $A + B = 60^\circ$   (Why?)      (2)
Solving (1) and (2), we get : $A = 45^\circ$ and $B = 15^\circ$.

blocks.text: 8.4 Trigonometric Ratios of Complementary Angles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall that two angles are said to be complementary
if their sum equals $90^\circ$. In $\Delta ABC$, right-angled at B,
do you see any pair of complementary angles?
(See Fig. 8.21)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since $\angle A + \angle C = 90^\circ$, they form such a pair. We have:

Paragraph
blocks.text: Now let us write the trigonometric ratios for $\angle C = 90^\circ - \angle A$.

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.label: Paragraph

You will find that AB is the side opposite and BC is the side adjacent to the angle

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 9 : Evaluate $\frac{\tan 65^{\circ}}{\cot 25^{\circ}}$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : We know : $\cot A = \tan (90^\circ - A)$
So, $\cot 25^\circ = \tan (90^\circ - 25^\circ) = \tan 65^\circ$
i.e., $\frac{\tan 65^\circ}{\cot 25^\circ} = \frac{\tan 65^\circ}{\tan 65^\circ} = 1$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 10} : If $\sin 3A = \cos (A - 26^\circ)$, where $3A$ is an acute angle, find the value of
$A$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
\underline{Solution} : We are given that $\sin 3A = \cos (A - 26^\circ)$. \hfill (1)
Since $\sin 3A = \cos (90^\circ - 3A)$, we can write (1) as
$$\cos (90^\circ - 3A) = \cos (A - 26^\circ)$$
Since $90^\circ - 3A$ and $A - 26^\circ$ are both acute angles, therefore,
$$90^\circ - 3A = A - 26^\circ$$
which gives
$$A = 29^\circ$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 11 : Express $\cot 85^{\circ} + \cos 75^{\circ}$ in terms of trigonometric ratios of angles
between $0^{\circ}$ and $45^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : $\cot 85^{\circ} + \cos 75^{\circ} = \cot (90^{\circ} - 5^{\circ}) + \cos (90^{\circ} - 15^{\circ})$
$= \tan 5^{\circ} + \sin 15^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.5 Trigonometric Identities

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may recall that an equation is called an identity
when it is true for all values of the variables involved.
Similarly, an equation involving trigonometric ratios
of an angle is called a trigonometric identity, if it is
true for all values of the angle(s) involved.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we will prove one trigonometric
identity, and use it further to prove other useful
trigonometric identities.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B (see Fig. 8.22), we have:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Dividing each term of (1) by $AC^2$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{AB^2}{AC^2} + \frac{BC^2}{AC^2} = \frac{AC^2}{AC^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{AB}{AC}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{BC}{AC}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{AC}{AC}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This is true for all $A$ such that $0^{\circ} \leq A \leq 90^{\circ}$. So, this is a trigonometric identity.
Let us now divide (1) by $AB^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{AB^2}{AB^2} + \frac{BC^2}{AB^2} = \frac{AC^2}{AB^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $\left(\frac{\Delta B}{AB}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{BC}{AB}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\Delta C}{AB}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $1 + \tan^{-1} \mathbf{A} = \sec^{-2} \mathbf{A}$ (3)

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: INTRODUCTION TO TRIGONOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Is this equation true for $A = 0^\circ$? Yes, it is. What about $A = 90^\circ$? Well, $\tan A$ and
sec $A$ are not defined for $A = 90^\circ$. So, (3) is true for all $A$ such that $0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us see what we get on dividing (1) by BC$^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{AB^2}{BC^2} + \frac{BC^2}{BC^2} = \frac{AC^2}{BC^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{AB}{BC}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{BC}{BC}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{AC}{BC}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that cosec A and cot A are not defined for $A = 0^\circ$. Therefore (4) is true for
all A such that $0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Using these identities, we can express each trigonometric ratio in terms of other
trigonometric ratios, i.e., if any one of the ratios is known, we can also determine the
values of other trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see how we can do this using these identities. Suppose we know that
$$\tan A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ Then, } \cot A = \sqrt{3} .$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Since, $\sec^2 A = 1 + \tan^2 A = 1 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$, $\sec A = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, and $\cos A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Again, $\sin A = \sqrt{1-\cos^2 A} = \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, cosec $A = 2$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 : Express the ratios $\cos A$, $\tan A$ and $\sec A$ in terms of $\sin A$.

Solution : Since $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$, therefore,

$$ \cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 A, \text{ i.e., } \cos A = \pm \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A} $$

This gives $\cos A = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}$ (Why?)

Hence, $\tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \frac{\sin A}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}}$ and $\sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{Example 14} : Prove that $\frac{\cot A - \cos A}{\cot A + \cos A} = \frac{\text{cosec A} - 1}{\text{cosec A} + 1}$

\textbf{Solution} : $\text{LHS} = \frac{\cot A - \cos A}{\cot A + \cos A} = \frac{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} - \cos A}{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} + \cos A}$

$= \frac{\cos A \left( \frac{1}{\sin A} - 1 \right)}{\cos A \left( \frac{1}{\sin A} + 1 \right)} = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{\sin A} - 1 \right)}{\left( \frac{1}{\sin A} + 1 \right)} = \frac{\text{cosec A} - 1}{\text{cosec A} + 1} = \text{RHS}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 15} : Prove that $\frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}$, using the identity
$\sec^2 \theta = 1 + \tan^2 \theta$.

\underline{Solution} : Since we will apply the identity involving $\sec \theta$ and $\tan \theta$, let us first
convert the LHS (of the identity we need to prove) in terms of $\sec \theta$ and $\tan \theta$ by
dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos \theta$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
LHS &= \frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{\tan \theta - 1 + \sec \theta}{\tan \theta + 1 - \sec \theta} \\
&= \frac{(\tan \theta + \sec \theta) - 1}{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta) + 1} = \frac{\{(\tan \theta + \sec \theta) - 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)\}}{\{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta) + 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}
\end{aligned}
$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{(\tan^2 \theta - \sec^2 \theta) - (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}{\{\tan \theta - \sec \theta + 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{-1 - \tan \theta + \sec \theta}{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta + 1)(\tan \theta - \sec \theta)} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{-1}{\tan \theta - \sec \theta} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}. $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the RHS of the identity, we are required to prove.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.6 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
$$ \sin A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \cos A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} $$
$$ \tan A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} $$
2. $\csc A = \frac{1}{\sin A} : \sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} : \tan A = \frac{1}{\cot A}, \tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}$ .
3. If one of the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle is known, the remaining trigonometric
   ratios of the angle can be easily determined.
4. The values of trigonometric ratios for angles $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.
5. The value of $\sin A$ or $\cos A$ never exceeds 1, whereas the value of $\sec A$ or $\csc A$ is
   always greater than or equal to 1.
6. $\sin(90^\circ - A) = \cos A, \cos(90^\circ - A) = \sin A$;
   $\tan(90^\circ - A) = \cot A, \cot(90^\circ - A) = \tan A$;
   $\sec(90^\circ - A) = \csc A, \csc(90^\circ - A) = \sec A$.
7. $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$,
   $\sec^2 A - \tan^2 A = 1$ for $0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ$,
   $\csc^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 A$ for $0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ$.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text:
SOME APPLICATIONS OF
TRIGONOMETRY 9

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous chapter, you have studied about trigonometric ratios. In this chapter,
you will be studying about some ways in which trigonometry is used in the life around
you. Trigonometry is one of the most ancient subjects studied by scholars all over the
world. As we have said in Chapter 8, trigonometry was invented because its need
arose in astronomy. Since then the astronomers have used it, for instance, to calculate
distances from the Earth to the planets and stars. Trigonometry is also used in geography
and in navigation. The knowledge of trigonometry is used to construct maps, determine
the position of an island in relation to the longitudes and latitudes.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Surveyors have used trigonometry for
centuries. One such large surveying project
of the nineteenth century was the 'Great
Trigonometric Survey' of British India
for which the two largest-ever theodolites
were built. During the survey in 1852, the
highest mountain in the world was
discovered. From a distance of over
160 km, the peak was observed from six
different stations. In 1856, this peak was
named after Sir George Everest, who had
commissioned and first used the giant
theodolites (see the figure alongside). The
theodolites are now on display in the
Museum of the Survey of India in
Dehradun.

A Theodolite
(Surveying instrument, which is based
on the Principles of trigonometry, is
used for measuring angles with a
rotating telescope)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will see how trigonometry is used for finding the heights and
distances of various objects, without actually measuring them.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.2 Heights and Distances

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider Fig. 8.1 of previous chapter, which is redrawn below in Fig. 9.1.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the
minar is called the line of sight. The student is looking at the top of the minar. The
angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the angle of
elevation of the top of the minar from the eye of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the **line of sight** is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point
in the object viewed by the observer. The **angle of elevation** of the point viewed is
the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point being viewed is
above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object
(see Fig. 9.2).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, consider the situation given in Fig. 8.2. The girl sitting on the balcony is
looking down at a flower pot placed on a stair of the temple. In this case, the line of
sight is below the horizontal level. The angle so formed by the line of sight with the
horizontal is called the angle of depression.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the angle of depression of a point on the object being viewed is the angle
formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point is below the horizontal
level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the point being viewed
(see Fig. 9.3).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, you may identify the lines of sight, and the angles so formed in Fig. 8.3.
Are they angles of elevation or angles of depression?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us refer to Fig. 9.1 again. If you want to find the height CD of the minar
without actually measuring it, what information do you need? You would need to know
the following:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar
(ii) the angle of elevation, $\angle BAC$, of the top of the minar
(iii) the height AE of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Assuming that the above three conditions are known, how can we determine the
height of the minar?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the figure, CD = CB + BD. Here, BD = AE, which is the height of the student.
To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of $\angle$ BAC or $\angle$ A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, the side BC is the opposite side in relation to the known $\angle$ A. Now,
which of the trigonometric ratios can we use? Which one of them has the two values
that we have and the one we need to determine? Our search narrows down to using
either $\tan A$ or $\cot A$, as these ratios involve AB and BC.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB}$ or $\cot A = \frac{AB}{BC}$, which on solving would give us BC.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: By adding AE to BC, you will get the height of the minar.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now let us explain the process, we have just discussed, by solving some problems.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground,
which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the
tower is found to be $60^{\circ}$. Find the height of the tower.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : First let us draw a simple diagram to
represent the problem (see Fig. 9.4). Here AB
represents the tower, CB is the distance of the point
from the tower and $\angle ACB$ is the angle of elevation.
We need to determine the height of the tower, i.e.,
AB. Also, ACB is a triangle, right-angled at B.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To solve the problem, we choose the trigonometric
ratio $\tan 60^{\circ}$ (or $\cot 60^{\circ}$), as the ratio involves AB
and BC.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.4

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\tan 60^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{BC}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\sqrt{3} = \frac{AB}{15}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $AB = 15\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the height of the tower is $15\sqrt{3}$ m.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 2} : An electrician has to repair an electric
fault on a pole of height 5 m. She needs to reach a
point 1.3m below the top of the pole to undertake the
repair work (see Fig. 9.5). What should be the length
of the ladder that she should use which, when inclined
at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal, would enable her
to reach the required position? Also, how far from
the foot of the pole should she place the foot of the
ladder? (You may take $\sqrt{3} = 1.73$)

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.5

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: SOME APPLICATIONS OF TRGONOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : In Fig. 9.5, the electrician is required to reach the point B on the pole AD.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, BC represents the ladder. We need to find its length, i.e., the hypotenuse of the
right triangle BDC.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, can you think which trigonometric ratio should we consider?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: It should be $\sin 60^\circ$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\mathrm{BD}}{\mathrm{BC}} = \sin 60^{\circ}$ or $\frac{3.7}{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $BC = \frac{3.7 \times 2}{\sqrt{3}} = 4.28 \text{ m (approx.)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: i.e., the length of the ladder should be 4.28 m.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\frac{\mathrm{DC}}{\mathrm{BD}} = \cot 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $DC = \frac{3.7}{\sqrt{3}} = 2.14 \text{ m (approx.)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, she should place the foot of the ladder at a distance of 2.14 m from the
pole.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m away
from a chimney. The angle of elevation of the top of
the chimney from her eyes is $45^\circ$. What is the height
of the chimney?

Solution : Here, AB is the chimney, CD the observer
and $\angle$ ADE the angle of elevation (see Fig. 9.6). In
this case, ADE is a triangle, right-angled at E and
we are required to find the height of the chimney.

We have $\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad AB = \Delta E + BE = AE + 1.5$

and $\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad DE = CB = 28.5 \text{ m}$

To determine AE, we choose a trigonometric ratio, which involves both AE and
DE. Let us choose the tangent of the angle of elevation.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\tan 45^\circ = \frac{AE}{DE}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AE = 28.5$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So the height of the chimney (AB) = $(28.5 + 1.5) \text{ m} = 30 \text{ m}.$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 4} : From a point P on the ground the angle of elevation of the top of a 10 m
tall building is $30^\circ$. A flag is hoisted at the top of the building and the angle of elevation
of the top of the flagstaff from P is $45^\circ$. Find the length of the flagstaff and the
distance of the building from the point P. (You may take $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : In Fig. 9.7, AB denotes the height of the building, BD the flagstaff and P
the given point. Note that there are two right triangles PAB and PAD. We are required
to find the length of the flagstaff, i.e., DB and the distance of the building from the
point P, i.e., PA.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since, we know the height of the building AB, we
will first consider the right $\Delta$ PAB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have $\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{AP}$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.7

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{10}{AP}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AP = 10\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: i.e., the distance of the building from P is $10\sqrt{3}$ m = 17.32 m.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Next, let us suppose DB = $x$ m. Then AD = $(10 + x)$ m.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, in right $\Delta$ PAD, $\tan 45^\circ = \frac{AD}{AP} = \frac{10+x}{10\sqrt{3}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $1 = \frac{10 + x}{10\sqrt{3}}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the length of the flagstaff is 7.32 m.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 : The shadow of a tower standing
on a level ground is found to be 40 m longer
when the Sun's altitude is $30^{\circ}$ than when it is
$60^{\circ}$. Find the height of the tower.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.8

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : In Fig. 9.8, AB is the tower and
BC is the length of the shadow when the
Sun's altitude is $60^{\circ}$, i.e., the angle of
elevation of the top of the tower from the tip
of the shadow is $60^{\circ}$ and DB is the length of
the shadow, when the angle of elevation is
$30^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let AB be $h$ m and BC be $x$ m. According to the question, DB is 40 m longer
than BC.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $DB = (40 + x) m$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we have two right triangles ABC and ABD.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: In $\Delta$ ABC, $\tan 60^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{BC}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $\sqrt{3} = \frac{h}{x}$ (1)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: In $\Delta ABD$, $\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{BD}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: From (1), we have $h = x\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Putting this value in (2), we get $(x\sqrt{3})\sqrt{3} = x + 40$, i.e., $3x = x + 40$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $h = 20\sqrt{3}$ [From (1)]

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the height of the tower is $20\sqrt{3}$ m.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building
from the top of a multi-storeyed building are $30^{\circ}$ and $45^{\circ}$, respectively. Find the height
of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between the two buildings.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : In Fig. 9.9, PC denotes the multi-
storeyed building and AB denotes the 8 m tall
building. We are interested to determine the
height of the multi-storeyed building, i.e., PC
and the distance between the two buildings,
i.e., AC.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.9

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Look at the figure carefully. Observe that
PB is a transversal to the parallel lines PQ
and BD. Therefore, $\angle QPB$ and $\angle PBD$ are
alternate angles, and so are equal.
So $\angle PBD = 30^\circ$. Similarly, $\angle PAC = 45^\circ$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In right $\Delta$ PBD, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\text{PD}}{\text{BD}} = \tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ or } \text{BD} = \text{PD} \sqrt{3} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In right $\Delta$ PAC, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\text{PC}}{\text{AC}} = \tan 45^\circ = 1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $PC = AC$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $PC = PD + DC$, therefore, $PD + DC = AC$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since, $AC = BD$ and $DC = AB = 8$ m, we get $PD + 8 = BD = PD\sqrt{3}$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $PD = \frac{8}{\sqrt{3}-1} = \frac{8(\sqrt{3}+1)}{(\sqrt{3}+1)(\sqrt{3}-1)} = 4(\sqrt{3}+1)m.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the height of the multi-storeyed building is $\{4(\sqrt{3} + 1) + 8\}m = 4(3 + \sqrt{3})m$
and the distance between the two buildings is also $4(3 + \sqrt{3})m$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : From a point on a bridge across a river, the angles of depression of
the banks on opposite sides of the river are $30^{\circ}$ and $45^{\circ}$, respectively. If the bridge
is at a height of 3 m from the banks, find the width of the river.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : In Fig 9.10, A and B
represent points on the bank on
opposite sides of the river, so that
AB is the width of the river. P is
a point on the bridge at a height
of 3 m, i.e., DP = 3 m. We are
interested to determine the width
of the river, which is the length
of the side AB of the $\Delta$ APB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $AB = AD + DB$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In right $\Delta$ APD, $\angle A = 30^\circ$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{PD}}{\text{AD}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{3}{AD}$ or $AD = 3\sqrt{3}$ m

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Also, in right $\Delta PBD$, $\angle B = 45^\circ$. So, $BD = PD = 3$ m.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $AB = BD + AD = 3 + 3\sqrt{3} = 3 (1 + \sqrt{3}) \text{ m.}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the width of the river is $3(\sqrt{3} + 1)$m.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 9.3 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1.  (i) The line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the
object viewed by the observer.

(ii) The angle of elevation of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight
with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise
our head to look at the object.

(iii) The angle of depression of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight
with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower
our head to look at the object.

2.  The height or length of an object or the distance between two distant objects can be
determined with the help of trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CIRCLES 10

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.] Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have studied in Class IX that a circle is a collection of all points in a plane
which are at a constant distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre). You have
also studied various terms related to a circle like chord, segment, sector, arc etc.
Let us now examine the different situations that can arise when a circle and a line
are given in a plane.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, let us consider a circle and a line PQ. There can be three possibilities given
in Fig. 10.1 below:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 10.1 (i), the line PQ and the circle have no common point. In this case,
PQ is called a non-intersecting line with respect to the circle. In Fig. 10.1 (ii), there
are two common points A and B that the line PQ and the circle have. In this case, we
call the line PQ a secant of the circle. In Fig. 10.1 (iii), there is only one point A which
is common to the line PQ and the circle. In this case, the line is called a tangent to the
circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You might have seen a pulley fitted over a well which is used
in taking out water from the well. Look at Fig. 10.2. Here the rope
on both sides of the pulley, if considered as a ray, is like a tangent
to the circle representing the pulley.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Is there any position of the line with respect to the circle
other than the types given above? You can see that there cannot
be any other type of position of the line with respect to the circle.
In this chapter, we will study about the existence of the tangents
to a circle and also study some of their properties.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.2 Tangent to a Circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, you have seen that a tangent* to a circle is a line that
intersects the circle at only one point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To understand the existence of the tangent to a circle at a point, let us perform
the following activities:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 1 : Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of the
circular wire so that it can rotate about the point P in a plane. Put the system on a table
and gently rotate the wire AB about the point P to get different positions of the straight
wire [see Fig. 10.3(i)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In various positions, the wire intersects the
circular wire at $P$ and at another point $Q_1$ or $Q_2$ or
$Q_3$, etc. In one position, you will see that it will
intersect the circle at the point $P$ only (see position
$A'B'$ of $AB$). This shows that a tangent exists at
the point $P$ of the circle. On rotating further, you
can observe that in all other positions of $AB$, it will
intersect the circle at $P$ and at another point, say $R_1$
or $R_2$ or $R_3$, etc. So, you can observe that there is
only one tangent at a point of the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
While doing activity above, you must have observed that as the position AB
moves towards the position $A' B'$, the common point, say $Q_1$, of the line AB and the
circle gradually comes nearer and nearer to the common point P. Ultimately, it coincides
with the point P in the position $A'B'$ of $A''B''$. Again note, what happens if 'AB' is
rotated rightwards about P? The common point $R_3$ gradually comes nearer and nearer
to P and ultimately coincides with P. So, what we see is:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end
points of its corresponding chord coincide.

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text:
*The word 'tangent' comes from the Latin word 'tangere', which means to touch and was
introduced by the Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 2 : On a paper, draw a circle and a
secant PQ of the circle. Draw various lines
parallel to the secant on both sides of it. You
will find that after some steps, the length of
the chord cut by the lines will gradually
decrease, i.e., the two points of intersection of
the line and the circle are coming closer and
closer [see Fig. 10.3(ii)]. In one case, it
becomes zero on one side of the secant and in
another case, it becomes zero on the other side
of the secant. See the positions $P'Q'$ and $P''Q''$
of the secant in Fig. 10.3 (ii). These are the
tangents to the circle parallel to the given secant
PQ. This also helps you to see that there cannot
be more than two tangents parallel to a given
secant.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 10.3 (ii)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This activity also establishes, what you must have observed, while doing
Activity 1, namely, a tangent is the secant when both of the end points of the
corresponding chord coincide.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the **point of contact**
[the point A in Fig. 10.1 (iii)]and the tangent is said to **touch** the circle at the
common point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now look around you. Have you seen a bicycle
or a cart moving? Look at its wheels. All the spokes
of a wheel are along its radii. Now note the position
of the wheel with respect to its movement on the
ground. Do you see any tangent anywhere?
(See Fig. 10.4). In fact, the wheel moves along a line
which is a tangent to the circle representing the wheel.
Also, notice that in all positions, the radius through
the point of contact with the ground appears to be at
right angles to the tangent (see Fig. 10.4). We shall
now prove this property of the tangent.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Theorem 10.1 : The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the
radius through the point of contact.
Proof : We are given a circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a
point P. We need to prove that OP is perpendicular to XY.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CIRCLES

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Take a point Q on XY other than P and join OQ (see Fig. 10.5).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The point Q must lie outside the circle.
(Why? Note that if Q lies inside the circle, XY
will become a secant and not a tangent to the
circle). Therefore, OQ is longer than the radius
OP of the circle. That is,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $OQ > OP.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since this happens for every point on the
line $XY$ except the point $P$, $OP$ is the
shortest of all the distances of the point $O$ to the
points of $XY$. So $OP$ is perpendicular to $XY$.
(as shown in Theorem A1.2.)

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. By theorem above, we can also conclude that at any point on a circle there can be
one and only one tangent.
2. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also sometimes called
the 'normal' to the circle at the point.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: EXERCISE 10.1

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. How many tangents can a circle have?
2. Fill in the blanks :
   (i) A tangent to a circle intersects it in _________ point (s).
   (ii) A line intersecting a circle in two points is called a ________.
   (iii) A circle can have _________ parallel tangents at the most.
   (iv) The common point of a tangent to a circle and the circle is called ________.
3. A tangent PQ at a point P of a circle of radius 5 cm meets a line through the centre O at
a point Q so that $OQ = 12$ cm. Length PQ is :
   (A) 12 cm      (B) 13 cm      (C) 8.5 cm      (D) $\sqrt{119}$ cm.
4. Draw a circle and two lines parallel to a given line such that one is a tangent and the
other, a secant to the circle.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.3 Number of Tangents from a Point on a Circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To get an idea of the number of tangents from a point on a circle, let us perform the
following activity:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 3 : Draw a circle on a paper. Take a
point P inside it. Can you draw a tangent to the
circle through this point? You will find that all
the lines through this point intersect the circle in
two points. So, it is not possible to draw any
tangent to a circle through a point inside it
[see Fig. 10.6 (i)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Next take a point P on the circle and draw
tangents through this point. You have already
observed that there is only one tangent to the
circle at such a point [see Fig. 10.6 (ii)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Finally, take a point P outside the circle and
try to draw tangents to the circle from this point.
What do you observe? You will find that you
can draw exactly two tangents to the circle
through this point [see Fig. 10.6 (iii)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We can summarise these facts as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 1 : There is no tangent to a circle passing
through a point lying inside the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 2 : There is one and only one tangent to a
circle passing through a point lying on the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 3 : There are exactly two tangents to a
circle through a point lying outside the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 10.6 (iii), $T_1$ and $T_2$ are the points of
contact of the tangents $PT_1$ and $PT_2$
respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The length of the segment of the tangent
from the external point P and the point of contact
with the circle is called the length of the tangent
from the point P to the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that in Fig. 10.6 (iii), $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$ are the lengths of the tangents from P to
the circle. The lengths $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$ have a common property. Can you find this?
Measure $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$. Are these equal? In fact, this is always so. Let us give a proof
of this fact in the following theorem.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CIRCULAR

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Theorem 10.2 : The lengths of tangents drawn
from an external point to a circle are equal.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\textbf{Proof} : We are given a circle with centre O, a
point P lying outside the circle and two tangents
PQ, PR on the circle from P (see Fig. 10.7). We
are required to prove that PQ = PR.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For this, we join OP, OQ and OR. Then
$\angle$ OQP and $\angle$ ORP are right angles, because
these are angles between the radii and tangents,
and according to Theorem 10.1 they are right
angles. Now in right triangles OQP and ORP,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$OQ = OR \quad \text{(Radii of the same circle)}$$
$$OP = OP \quad \text{(Common)}$$
$$Therefore, \quad \Delta OQP \cong \Delta ORP \quad \text{(RHS)}$$
$$\text{This gives} \quad PQ = PR \quad \text{(CPCT)}$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. The theorem can also be proved by using the Pythagoras Theorem as follows:
$$PQ^2 = OP^2 - OQ^2 = OP^2 - OR^2 = PR^2 \ (As \ OQ = OR)$$
which gives $PQ = PR$.
2. Note also that $\angle OPQ = \angle OPR$. Therefore, OP is the angle bisector of $\angle QPR$,
i.e., the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us take some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 1} : Prove that in two concentric circles,
the chord of the larger circle, which touches the
smaller circle, is bisected at the point of contact.
Solution : We are given two concentric circles
$C_1$ and $C_2$ with centre O and a chord AB of the
larger circle C, which touches the smaller circle
$C_2$ at the point P (see Fig. 10.8). We need to prove
that $AP = BP$.
Let us join OP. Then, AB is a tangent to $C_2$ at P
and OP is its radius. Therefore, by Theorem 10.1,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now AB is a chord of the circle $C_1$ and OP $\perp$ AB. Therefore, OP is the bisector of the
chord AB, as the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $AP = BP$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn
to a circle with centre O from an external point T.
Prove that $\angle PTQ = 2 \angle OPQ$.

Solution : We are given a circle with centre O,
an external point T and two tangents TP and TQ
to the circle, where P, Q are the points of contact
(see Fig. 10.9). We need to prove that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\angle PTQ = 2 \angle OPQ$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let $\angle PTQ = \theta$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, by Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ. So, TPQ is an isosceles triangle.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\angle TPQ = \angle TQP = \frac{1}{2}(180^\circ - \theta) = 90^\circ - \frac{1}{2}\theta$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, by Theorem 10.1, $\angle OPT = 90^\circ$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle OPQ = \angle OPT - \angle TPQ = 90^\circ - \left( 90^\circ - \frac{1}{2}\theta \right)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{1}{2} \theta = \frac{1}{2} \angle PTQ $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $\angle PTQ = 2 \angle OPQ$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\underline{Example 3} : PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a
circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q
intersect at a point T (see Fig. 10.10). Find the
length TP.

\underline{Solution} : Join OT. Let it intersect PQ at the
point R. Then $\Delta$ TPQ is isosceles and TO is the
angle bisector of $\angle PTQ$. So, $OT \perp PQ$
and therefore, OT bisects PQ which gives
$PR = RQ = 4$ cm.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $OR = \sqrt{OP^2 - PR^2} = \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} \text{ cm} = 3 \text{ cm}.$

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CIRCLES

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\angle TPR + \angle RPO = 90^\circ = \angle TPR + \angle PTR$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle \text{RPO} = \angle \text{PTR}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, right triangle TRP is similar to the right triangle PRO by AA similarity.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{PO}} = \frac{\text{RP}}{\text{RO}}$, i.e., $\frac{\text{TP}}{5} = \frac{4}{3}$ or $\text{TP} = \frac{20}{3}$ cm.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Note : TP can also be found by using the Pythagoras Theorem, as follows:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Let $TP = x$ and $TR = y$. Then

$x^2 = y^2 + 16$ (Taking right $\Delta$ PRT) (1)

$x^2 + 5^2 = (y + 3)^2$ (Taking right $\Delta$ OPT) (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Subtracting (1) from (2), we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$25 = 6y - 7 \quad \text{or} \quad y = \frac{32}{6} = \frac{16}{3}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $x^2 = \left(\frac{16}{3}\right)^2 + 16 = \frac{16}{9}(16 + 9) = \frac{16 \times 25}{9}$ [From (1)]

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you have done certain constructions using a straight edge (ruler) and a
compass, e.g., bisecting an angle, drawing the perpendicular bisector of a line segment,
some constructions of triangles etc. and also gave their justifications. In this chapter,
we shall study some more constructions by using the knowledge of the earlier
constructions. You would also be expected to give the mathematical reasoning behind
why such constructions work.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.2 Division of a Line Segment

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose a line segment is given and you have to divide it in a given ratio, say $3 : 2$. You
may do it by measuring the length and then marking a point on it that divides it in the
given ratio. But suppose you do not have any way of measuring it precisely, how
would you find the point? We give below two ways for finding such a point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Construction 11.1 : To divide a line segment in a given ratio.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Given a line segment AB, we want to divide it in the ratio $m : n$, where both $m$ and
$n$ are positive integers. To help you to understand it, we shall take $m=3$ and $n=2$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of Construction :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Draw any ray AX, making an acute angle with AB.
2. Locate 5 ($= m + n$) points $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $A_4$ and
$A_5$ on AX so that $AA_1 = A_1A_2 = A_2A_3 = A_3A_4$
$= A_4A_5$.
3. Join $BA_5$.
4. Through the point $A_5$ ($m = 3$), draw a line
parallel to $A_3B$ (by making an angle equal to
$\angle AA_3B$) at $A_5$ intersecting AB at the point C
(see Fig. 11.1). Then, $AC : CB = 3 : 2$.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CONSTRUCTIONS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us see how this method gives us the required division.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since $A_1C$ is parallel to $A_1B$, therefore,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{AA_3}{A_3A_5} = \frac{AC}{CB} \qquad \text{(By the Basic Proportionality Theorem)} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: By construction, $\frac{AA_3}{A_3A_3} = \frac{3}{2}$. Therefore, $\frac{AC}{CB} = \frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This shows that C divides AB in the ratio $3:2$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Alternative Method

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of Construction :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Draw any ray AX making an acute angle with AB.      Fig. 11.2
2. Draw a ray BY parallel to AX by making $\angle ABY$ equal to $\angle BAX$.
3. Locate the points $A_1, A_2, A_3$ ($m=3$) on AX and $B_1, B_2$ ($n=2$) on BY such that
   $AA_1 = A_1A_2 = A_2A_3 = BB_1 = B_1B_2$.
4. Join $A_3B_2$. Let it intersect AB at a point C (see Fig. 11.2).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then $AC : CB = 3 : 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Why does this method work? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here $\Delta AA_3C$ is similar to $\Delta BB_2C$. (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\frac{AA_3}{BB_2} = \frac{AC}{BC}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Since by construction, $\frac{\mathrm{AA}_3}{\mathrm{BB}_2} = \frac{3}{2}$ therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In fact, the methods given above work for dividing the line segment in any ratio.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We now use the idea of the construction above for constructing a triangle similar
to a given triangle whose sides are in a given ratio with the corresponding sides of the
given triangle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Construction 11.2 : To construct a triangle similar to a given triangle as per
given scale factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This construction involves two different situations. In one, the triangle to be
constructed is smaller and in the other it is larger than the given triangle. Here, the
scale factor means the ratio of the sides of the triangle to be constructed with the
corresponding sides of the given triangle (see also Chapter 6). Let us take the following
examples for understanding the constructions involved. The same methods would
apply for the general case also.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Construct a triangle similar to a given triangle ABC with its sides equal
to $\frac{3}{4}$ of the corresponding sides of the triangle ABC (i.e., of scale factor $\frac{3}{4}$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Given a triangle ABC, we are required to construct another triangle whose
sides are $\frac{3}{4}$ of the corresponding sides of the triangle ABC.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of Construction :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Draw any ray BX making an acute angle
with BC on the side opposite to the vertex
A.

2. Locate 4 (the greater of 3 and 4 in $\frac{3}{4}$)
points $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$ and $B_4$ on BX so that
$BB_1 = B_1B_2 = B_2B_3 = B_3B_4$.

3. Join $B_4C$ and draw a line through $B_3$ (the
3rd point, 3 being smaller of 3 and 4 in
$\frac{3}{4}$) parallel to $B_4C$ to intersect BC at $C'$.

4. Draw a line through $C'$ parallel
to the line CA to intersect BA at $A'$
(see Fig. 11.3).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then, $\Delta ABC'$ is the required triangle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us now see how this construction gives the required triangle.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: By Construction 11.1, $\frac{BC'}{C'C} = \frac{3}{1}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{BC}'} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}' + \mathrm{C}'\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{BC}'} = 1 + \frac{\mathrm{C}'\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{BC}'} = 1 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$, i.e., $\frac{\mathrm{BC}'}{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{3}{4}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Also C'A' is parallel to CA. Therefore, $\Delta$ A'BC' - $\Delta$ ABC.   (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{A'B}{AB} = \frac{A'C}{AC} = \frac{BC'}{BC} = \frac{3}{4}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Construct a triangle similar to a given triangle ABC with its sides equal
to $\frac{5}{3}$ of the corresponding sides of the triangle ABC (i.e., of scale factor $\frac{5}{3}$).

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CONSTRUCTIONS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Given a triangle ABC, we are required to construct a triangle whose sides
are $\frac{5}{3}$ of the corresponding sides of $\Delta$ ABC.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of Construction :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Draw any ray BX making an acute angle with BC on the side opposite to the
vertex A.

2. Locate 5 points (the greater of 5 and 3 in $\frac{5}{3}$ ) B$_1$, B$_2$, B$_3$, B$_4$ and B$_5$ on BX so that
$BB_1 = B_1B_2 = B_2B_3 = B_3B_4 = B_4B_5$.

3. Join B$_3$(the 3rd point, 3 being smaller of 3 and 5 in $\frac{5}{3}$ ) to C and draw a line through
B$_5$ parallel to B$_3$C, intersecting the extended line segment BC at C'.

4. Draw a line through C' parallel to CA
intersecting the extended line segment BA at
A' (see Fig. 11.4).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then $A'BC'$ is the required triangle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For justification of the construction, note that
$\Delta ABC \sim \Delta A'BC'$. (Why ?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{C}'} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{BC}'}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{But, } \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{BC}'} = \frac{\text{BB}_3}{\text{BB}_3} = \frac{3}{5}, $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{BC'}{BC} = \frac{5}{3}$, and, therefore, $\frac{AB}{AB} = \frac{A'C'}{AC} = \frac{BC'}{BC} = \frac{5}{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : In Examples 1 and 2, you could take a ray making an acute angle with AB
or AC and proceed similarly.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: EXERCISE 11.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In each of the following, give the justification of the construction also:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Draw a line segment of length 7.6 cm and divide it in the ratio 5 : 8. Measure the two
parts.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
2. Construct a triangle of sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm and then a triangle similar to it whose
sides are $\frac{2}{3}$ of the corresponding sides of the first triangle.

3. Construct a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm and then another triangle whose

5. Draw a triangle ABC with side BC = 6 cm, AB = 5 cm and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$. Then construct

6. Draw a triangle ABC with side BC = 7 cm, $\angle B = 45^\circ$, $\angle A = 105^\circ$. Then, construct a
triangle whose sides are $\frac{4}{3}$ times the corresponding sides of $\Delta$ ABC.

7. Draw a right triangle in which the sides (other than hypotenuse) are of lengths 4 cm and
